Beyond Search-Imitation:
Prior-Directed Exploration for Searchless Chess

Szymon Miłosz*    Piotr Duch    Szymon Grabowski Affiliation: Institute of Applied Computer Science, Lodz University of Technology Affiliation: *Corresponding author: szymon.milosz@dokt.p.lodz.pl
Abstract

Searchless chess networks reach human master strength from a single forward pass by imitating a stronger teacher: the strongest, Leela Chess Zero’s (Lc0) released Chessformer, distills the visit counts of an AlphaZero-style Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). Imitating a search is a poor proxy for playing without one, so we fine-tune for single-pass strength with self-play reinforcement learning (RL). Its exploration is usually supplied by an entropy bonus—the reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence to uniform. We replace it with a forward, mass-covering KL toward the network’s own MCTS prior—prior-directed exploration—so exploration covers the moves the prior judges promising, and pair it with an entropy-adaptive sampling temperature, set by the value head’s outcome uncertainty, that sharpens once a position is decided. In about two thousand steps it raises puzzle accuracy from 93.9%93.9\% to 94.9%94.9\% on a 100,000100{,}000-puzzle suite and mate-in-four accuracy from 77%77\% to 81%81\% while holding searchless strength at or slightly above the base. Measuring tactical accuracy and playing strength together across a matched-compute sweep, we find the two dissociate: accuracy gains fall in a one-point band while ratings straddle the base, and a control fine-tuned on puzzles alone posts the study’s largest tactical gains while shedding roughly 260260 Elo—a better puzzle-solver is not thereby a stronger player. Distribution-level measurements show what anchoring buys: without a regularizer self-play collapses onto a single line of play, and the puzzles newly solved are the near misses whose winning move the prior kept alive. The forward-KL prior tops the rating ladder, statistically tied with a reverse-KL anchor that concentrates twice as hard and drops the hardest solutions the mass-covering prior keeps in support.

Keywords: searchless chess; self-play reinforcement learning; exploration; Kullback–Leibler regularization; policy gradient; transformer policy networks
Code: https://github.com/szmilosz/prior-directed-exploration

1  Introduction

A recent line of work builds chess networks that play at up to human master strength11 1 We use “master” conservatively and avoid “grandmaster,” which we think outruns the evidence. Strength here is pool-dependent: Ruoss et al. (2024) rate the same searchless agent at 28952895 against humans in the Lichess blitz pool but at 22992299 in an engine tournament, and the interpretability study we build on titles our exact checkpoint “grandmaster-level” (Lin et al., 2026). Labels of that kind rest on online blitz or engine-pool ratings: the only human-facing evidence in this line is blitz play on Lichess, and the sole reported game record outside it is a five-game exhibition against a 21002100-rated player. Online pools run well above the over-the-board scale at equal strength, and none of these networks has been evaluated at classical time controls, where such a claim would have to be settled. Our claims are relative to the base network and do not turn on the absolute label. while almost eliminating test-time search: the move comes from a single forward pass of a policy (Monroe et al., 2026), a one-ply value lookup over the legal children (Ruoss et al., 2024), or a fixed, shallow decoding or beam procedure standing in for a tree search (Ye et al., 2025; Hamara et al., 2025). Every one of them is trained by imitation: a network is fit to a stronger but slower teacher and then frozen. Our starting point is the strongest, the Chessformer architecture (Monroe et al., 2026) as instantiated and trained by Leela Chess Zero (Lc0) (The LCZero Authors, 2018); it is obtained by supervised distillation of AlphaZero-style self-play data, fitting its policy head to the search’s MCTS visit-count distribution and its value head to game outcomes. We write “Chessformer” for this released network from here on. Imitating a search is mismatched with playing without one in two ways. The target is mismatched, because the visit-count distribution is only a noisy proxy for the move that maximizes win probability under direct, searchless play. The state distribution is mismatched, because the training games were produced with search while the weaker searchless policy, left to its own devices, reaches a different distribution of positions, the covariate shift familiar from imitation learning. Self-play RL removes both at once: it optimizes a win/draw/loss reward for searchless strength on data drawn from the searchless policy’s own play. We use it to push Chessformer beyond its search-imitation training.

Interpretability studies of Lc0’s transformer chess networks make the target mismatch concrete: these networks carry rich internal computation—with evidence even of learned look-ahead to future optimal moves (Jenner et al., 2024)—yet on tactical puzzles with a single winning move, that move is often computed in the intermediate layers only for the final layer to override it in favor of a safer, positional alternative; a targeted intervention against this late-layer safety bias has been shown to reverse the override for a majority of the suppressed wins (Sandmann et al., 2025) (observed on a smaller network of the same square-token lineage rather than on our exact checkpoint; Appendix B). Because searchless play commits to the arg​max\argmax, such an override costs strength outright, and we conjecture that fine-tuning on game outcomes restores the move’s rank—reaching through training the correction their activation steering reaches at inference.

Reinforcement learning improves a policy only to the extent that it explores, and policy-gradient methods sustain exploration with an entropy bonus that keeps the action distribution spread out (Williams, 1992; Williams and Peng, 1991; Mnih et al., 2016; Schulman et al., 2017; Haarnoja et al., 2018). The entropy bonus is indifferent to which moves are worth trying. Up to an additive constant it is the negative KL divergence −DKL(πθ∥𝒰)-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}\,\big\|\,\mathcal{U}\right) to the uniform distribution 𝒰\mathcal{U}, so it pushes probability onto all legal moves, including the many that no strong player would consider. With a large branching factor this spends the exploration budget on obviously bad moves and gives a weak, undirected signal; the same uninformed spreading, and its converse entropy collapse, are live concerns in language-model RL (Cui et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025).

A far better reference is already available at no extra cost: the base network’s own policy. The network was trained to match the MCTS visit-count distributions of a self-play search, so a single forward pass already returns a search-derived map of the moves worth examining—not the search itself, but the network’s distilled approximation of it. We use this policy πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} as the exploration reference, replacing the entropy bonus with a forward, mass-covering KL penalty DKL(πbase∥πθ)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\theta}\right) toward it. Direction is what turns a divergence into an exploration signal: the mass-covering KL diverges whenever the policy drops a move the prior considers promising, forcing the policy to keep covering the prior’s informed support, whereas the mode-seeking DKL(πθ∥πbase)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\right), the anchoring penalty of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and from verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Ouyang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024), would let the policy collapse onto one move. Using the mass-covering direction for exploration has appeared recently in language-model RL (Deng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025); we adapt it as a drop-in replacement for the entropy bonus, toward a fixed search-derived prior, in searchless chess. We call the mechanism prior-directed exploration; Section 4 places it among the alternatives.

Prior-directed exploration helps only when the reference is itself exploratory, spreading mass over several promising moves rather than one, so that there is breadth worth covering. Search-derived policies satisfy this by construction, which is why the MCTS prior plays a double role here: a noisy pointwise target for imitation, but an excellent exploratory reference for RL. The late-layer demotion described above (Sandmann et al., 2025) illustrates this split directly: the winning move the output passes over is not erased but re-ranked just below the top, so it persists in the policy’s distribution with substantial mass—failing as a pointwise target yet remaining precisely the support a coverage-preserving penalty can keep while the reward lifts it back (Section 3.5 measures this: the solution sits at rank two in 71%71\% of the base’s failures). During fine-tuning the win/draw/loss reward re-sharpens the policy within the prior’s support toward what actually wins, while the forward KL keeps it from collapsing (Figure 1 previews the outcome on exact mates).

Contributions.

  • •

    We cast strengthening a searchless network as moving beyond search-imitation and instantiate it as self-play RL that optimizes Chessformer’s single-pass strength directly, addressing the noisy-target and distribution-shift mismatches of imitation, in a single-step self-play recipe: truncated importance sampling and a one-step temporal-difference (TD(0)) value head with an exponential-moving-average (EMA) target (Sections 2.3–3).

  • •

    For exploration we replace the entropy bonus with a forward, mass-covering KL toward the network’s own MCTS visit-count prior, prior-directed exploration, adapting a mechanism recently used in language-model RL (Deng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025) to a fixed external prior whose support is worth covering; we further argue (Appendix C) that a search-distilled prior is exploratory by construction (Section 2.2).

  • •

    We introduce an entropy-adaptive sampling temperature that sets each move’s temperature to the value head’s win/draw/loss uncertainty, so self-play terminates once a position is decided yet stays exploratory while it is live (Section 2.3).

  • •

    Empirically, where the interpretability studies of these networks probe them almost entirely through tactical puzzles, we show prior-directed fine-tuning improves both tactics and searchless strength—modestly on strength, in about two thousand steps. We further quantify, under matched compute, that tactical accuracy and playing strength dissociate, so the coupling rests on anchoring exploration to the prior rather than on tactical optimization alone; and we show the tactical gains are retention-gated: fine-tuning promotes near misses the base still ranked second or third and recovers nothing whose solution the base had driven below πbase≈0.05\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\!\approx\!0.05 (Section 3).

  • •

    We define and measure two coverage-versus-collapse diagnostics—trajectory coverage ΩKN\Omega^{N}_{K} and the solution probability of sampling a ground-truth winning line in one pass. Both split as the mechanism predicts: the unregularized policy collapses onto a single opening line, and the mode-seeking anchor concentrates about twice as hard as the forward prior and drops the hardest solutions, where the forward prior retains them (Section 3).

2  Method

2.1  Background: policy gradients and entropy regularization

We work with policy-gradient RL: a stochastic policy πθ​(a∣s)\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s) is improved by ascending the objective 𝔼(s,a)​[A⁡(s,a)​log⁡πθ​(a∣s)]\mathbb{E}_{(s,a)}[A(s,a)\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)], with A⁡(s,a)A(s,a) an estimate of the advantage of the sampled move. Unregularized, this update is self-reinforcing. It keeps raising the probability of whatever currently looks best and drives πθ\pi_{\theta} toward a deterministic policy that no longer samples alternatives, often before the best move has been found. The failure is self-sealing: a policy-gradient update credits only the moves it actually samples, so once a move’s probability reaches zero its reward is never observed again and no gradient can restore it—exploration must keep candidate moves sampled for their rewards to remain discoverable. A regularizer that sustains exploration is therefore added; the standard one is the entropy bonus λ𝔼s[H(πθ(⋅∣s))]\lambda\,\mathbb{E}_{s}[\Ent(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s))] with λ>0\lambda>0. Up to an additive constant it penalizes the KL divergence to the uniform distribution 𝒰s\mathcal{U}_{s} over the legal moves 𝒜⁡(s)\mathcal{A}(s),

H(πθ(⋅∣s))=log|𝒜(s)|−DKL(πθ(⋅∣s)∥𝒰s),\Ent(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s))=\log|\mathcal{A}(s)|-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)\,\big\|\,\mathcal{U}_{s}\right), (1)

with the optimized policy as the first argument. We follow the convention in which the forward (inclusive) KL places the fixed reference first and the reverse (exclusive) KL places the optimized policy first. Entropy regularization is thus the reverse KL toward a single, fixed, and maximally uninformative reference. The choice of direction, central to our method, is the subject of the next subsection.

2.2  Prior-directed exploration via a forward-KL prior

The uniform reference encodes nothing about the task. When a strong policy πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} is on hand, it describes far better where exploration should go, because it already places mass on the moves worth trying. We replace the entropy bonus with a penalty that pulls πθ\pi_{\theta} toward πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} in the forward, mass-covering direction,

ℛ(θ)=𝔼s[DKL(πbase(⋅∣s)∥πθ(⋅∣s))]=𝔼s[∑a∈𝒜⁡(s)πbase(a∣s)logπbase​(a∣s)πθ​(a∣s)],\mathcal{R}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{s}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\cdot\mid s)\,\big\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)\right)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{s}\!\Big[\textstyle\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}(s)}\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(a\mid s)\log\tfrac{\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(a\mid s)}{\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}\Big], (2)

which, added with weight β>0\beta>0 in place of the entropy bonus, gives the policy objective

ℒπ(θ)=−𝔼(s,a)[A(s,a)logπθ(a∣s)]+β𝔼s[DKL(πbase(⋅∣s)∥πθ(⋅∣s))].\mathcal{L}_{\pi}(\theta)=-\,\mathbb{E}_{(s,a)}\!\left[A(s,a)\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\right]+\beta\,\mathbb{E}_{s}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\cdot\mid s)\,\big\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)\right)\right]. (3)

Why the forward direction.

Direction is the crux, and Figure 2 lays out the asymmetry in full. Our penalty DKL(πbase∥πθ)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\theta}\right) takes the forward, mass-covering direction—in the usual terminology zero-avoiding—so minimizing it forces the policy to keep probability on every move the prior deems promising, which is exactly what an exploration signal should do—it prevents collapse to a near-deterministic strategy, and the moves it must cover are the prior’s high-probability ones rather than the whole action set. The reverse KL DKL(πθ∥πbase)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\right) is mode-seeking and zero-forcing (Minka, 2005) instead—the anchoring penalty of KL-regularized policy optimization, from behavior priors to RLHF and RLVR (Galashov et al., 2019; Ouyang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024; Tirumala et al., 2022). That is the right property for the anchor’s job, which is to confine the policy to a trusted reference’s support—in RLHF so that a learned reward cannot be over-optimized by drifting off it (reward hacking)—but as an exploration driver it would license the very collapse we are trying to prevent: the two uses want opposite failure modes from the same divergence. We are deliberate about the word “exploration”: the forward KL sustains coverage of the prior’s promising moves and prevents collapse onto one of them, but being zero where πbase​(a)→0\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(a)\to 0 it cannot drive discovery of strong moves outside the prior’s support. It preserves prior-anchored breadth rather than seeking novelty, unlike the intrinsic-motivation methods of Section 4.

Relation to entropy regularization, and the requirement on the prior.

Entropy regularization is the reverse KL to the uniform reference (Equation (1)), and even there the directions are not interchangeable: the forward KL to uniform DKL(𝒰∥πθ)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\mathcal{U}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\theta}\right) is the label-smoothing penalty (Pereyra et al., 2017), not the entropy bonus. Both share a minimizer against a uniform reference, so either one merely spreads mass over all moves; prior-directed exploration keeps the mass-covering direction and swaps that uninformative reference for the prior, turning uniform spreading into coverage of the prior’s promising moves. Because the penalty forces πθ\pi_{\theta} to cover the support of πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}}, it is only as useful as that support: a near-deterministic expert would pull the policy onto one move and reproduce collapse, so the method pairs naturally with priors that are themselves products of exploration, such as MCTS visit-count policies.

Our prior meets that condition by construction, in two steps. First, the targets the search exports are high-entropy exactly where exploration matters: the predictor-guided upper-confidence rule (PUCT) keeps visiting every move with appreciable prior until its count catches up, so the exported distribution πmcts​(a∣s)∝N​(s,a)1/τ\pi_{\mathrm{mcts}}(a\mid s)\propto N(s,a)^{1/\tau} retains mass on several moves wherever more than one is reasonable and sharpens only where the search itself is confident. Second, the released network was fit to those targets by cross-entropy, which is the forward KL DKL(πmcts∥πbase)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\mathrm{mcts}}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\right) up to the target’s own entropy—the same mass-covering direction we use here—so a network that collapsed onto one move would pay a large loss at every position where the search spread its visits, and the breadth transfers to the single-pass policy. The prior we cover is therefore the product of a search, not a runtime search itself, and the argument does not turn on the particular search variant; Appendix C gives it in full. How much coverage results under the full objective also depends on β\beta and the reward scale (GX-Chen et al., 2025), which we set empirically.

A second enabling condition is computational: the forward KL needs the reference’s full distribution at each state, which is immediate for an enumerable categorical over the legal moves but expensive for a language model over its vocabulary, one reason the reverse direction is the default in large-scale post-training (Appendix E).

2.3  A single-step self-play recipe for searchless chess

We instantiate prior-directed exploration as self-play fine-tuning of Chessformer for searchless play. The policy, its self-play rollouts, and the value bootstrap all use a single network evaluation per position, with no tree search at training or test time, so the objective matches searchless deployment. The reference πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} is the frozen Chessformer of Section 1; we initialize the online policy πθ\pi_{\theta} from it. The value head outputs a win/draw/loss (WDL) distribution, summarized by the scalar score vθ​(s)=pθW​(s)+12​pθD​(s)∈[0,1]v_{\theta}(s)=p^{\mathrm{W}}_{\theta}(s)+\tfrac{1}{2}p^{\mathrm{D}}_{\theta}(s)\in[0,1]. We estimate the advantage of a move aa from ss to s′=T⁡(s,a)s^{\prime}=T(s,a) by a one-step TD(0) residual,

A⁡(s,a)=(1−vθ¯​(s′))−vθ​(s),A(s,a)=\big(1-v_{\bar{\theta}}(s^{\prime})\big)-v_{\theta}(s), (4)

where θ¯\bar{\theta} are exponential-moving-average (EMA) target weights and 1−vθ¯​(s′)1-v_{\bar{\theta}}(s^{\prime}) converts the successor score to the moving player’s view, a flip licensed by the zero-sum, symmetric self-play. Both AA and the importance weight introduced below are computed when the transition is collected and enter the loss as constants, so no gradient reaches vθ​(s)v_{\theta}(s) through the policy term. The value loss regresses vθ​(s)v_{\theta}(s) toward the same bootstrapped target that enters AA, and the head starts near-consistent, so 𝔼⁡[A]≈0\mathbb{E}[A]\approx 0 and mean-centering would subtract almost nothing; we also avoid variance scaling, which would rescale the advantage’s natural win-probability units (Appendix E). Data collection and optimization alternate synchronously: each batch is generated by the current parameters and consumed by one optimizer step (gradients accumulated over micro-batches), with no replay buffer and no additional epochs. The parameters that collect a batch therefore coincide with the parameters it updates, the probability ratio of Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is identically one, and PPO clipping (Schulman et al., 2017) is inert: the update reduces exactly to the advantage-weighted gradient of Equation (3) (derived in Appendix E). This is the familiar fact that one inner epoch turns PPO into a baseline-corrected policy gradient; we present it as a simplification, not a stability mechanism, since dropping the clip leaves the per-step change bounded only by the small layerwise learning rates; the EMA target smooths the value estimates that feed AA but does not itself bound the policy step.

Entropy-adaptive sampling temperature.

The forward-KL prior shapes where the policy explores; within a game we also control how decisively it plays. Sampling every move from πθ\pi_{\theta} leaves decided positions needlessly stochastic and wastes rollouts that could begin fresh games; it also misdirects the update, since converting a decided position is something the supervised base already does well, and both the rollout budget and the learning signal are better spent on the contested positions where the outcome is still in doubt. AlphaZero-style self-play handles this with a ply-indexed temperature, sampling for the first plies and then playing greedily (Silver et al., 2018), but the move number is a coarse proxy for whether a position is actually settled. We instead tie the temperature to the value head’s own uncertainty, the entropy of its WDL distribution,

τ(s)=H(𝐩(s))=−∑o∈{W,D,L}po(s)lnpo(s)∈[0,ln3],\tau(s)=\Ent(\mathbf{p}(s))=-\!\!\sum_{o\in\{\mathrm{W},\mathrm{D},\mathrm{L}\}}\!\!p^{o}(s)\ln p^{o}(s)\in[0,\ln 3], (5)

and sample from the tempered behavior policy

μ⁡(a∣s)∝πθ​(a∣s)1/τ⁡(s),a∈𝒜⁡(s),\mu(a\mid s)\propto\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)^{1/\tau(s)},\qquad a\in\mathcal{A}(s), (6)

with μ→arg​maxa⁡πθ​(a∣s)\mu\to\argmax_{a}\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s) as τ→0\tau\to 0.

We use the raw entropy rather than normalizing it: the maximum WDL entropy is ln⁡3≈1.10\ln 3\approx 1.10, so the unnormalized temperature spans [0,ln⁡3]≈[0,1.1][0,\ln 3]\approx[0,1.1], close enough to the unit interval to behave as a temperature; with kk outcomes one would divide by ln⁡k\ln k to fix the range, which matters when kk is large. Because τ≤ln⁡3\tau\leq\ln 3, the exponent 1/τ1/\tau never falls below 0.910.91: μ\mu essentially never flattens πθ\pi_{\theta}, it only withdraws stochasticity from decided positions, and the spread it preserves elsewhere is the spread the forward-KL term maintains. Decided positions have near-one-hot WDL, so τ→0\tau\to 0 and μ\mu sharpens to finish the game quickly, reliable because the base value head is already strong at conversion, while positions whose outcome is genuinely uncertain keep τ\tau large and μ≈πθ\mu\approx\pi_{\theta}, preserving exploration where the learning signal is richest (Figure 3). The proxy is outcome uncertainty, not move criticality, so μ\mu also sharpens in the relatively rare position whose outcome is settled yet whose move choice still matters; there it falls back on the base policy’s top move, dependable given the base’s conversion strength but not infallible. Sampling from μ\mu rather than πθ\pi_{\theta} makes the batch off-policy, which we correct with a truncated importance weight in the style of V-trace (Espeholt et al., 2018); τ\tau is computed from the EMA value head for stability (Appendix E).

Overall objective.

The value head is trained by the same one-step bootstrap: it regresses its WDL prediction at ss onto the point-of-view-flipped EMA prediction at s′s^{\prime} by cross-entropy ℒV\mathcal{L}_{V} (Appendix E). The online network minimizes

ℒ(θ)=−𝔼(s,a)​[A⁡(s,a)​log⁡πθ​(a∣s)]⏟policy gradient+β𝔼s[DKL(πbase∥πθ)]+cvℒV(θ),\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\underbrace{-\,\mathbb{E}_{(s,a)}\!\left[A(s,a)\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\right]}_{\text{policy gradient}}+\beta\,\mathbb{E}_{s}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\theta}\right)\right]+c_{v}\,\mathcal{L}_{V}(\theta), (7)

where the forward-KL term replaces the entropy bonus and cv>0c_{v}>0 balances policy and value. Figure 4 diagrams this loop and Algorithm 1 states it in full; data generation, the truncated importance weight, and the single-step reduction are in Appendices D and E.

3  Experiments

We ask whether prior-directed exploration improves a searchless engine over its base—in tactical accuracy and in playing strength, without the regression that tactical optimization alone can cause—holding the rest of the pipeline fixed. The experiments test four things: whether self-play RL moves the supervised base beyond search-imitation in tactics and in strength; whether tactical accuracy and playing strength move together or dissociate across exploration terms; how the forward-KL prior compares with the entropy bonus, a reverse-KL anchor, and no regularizer at equal compute; and how much each component of the recipe contributes.

3.1  Setup and metrics

Setup and conditions.

Starting from the same frozen Chessformer reference, the publicly released Lc0 checkpoint BT4-1024x15x32h-swa-6147500 (architecture in Appendix B), we fine-tune with the procedure of Section 2.3, varying only the exploration term and holding the network, optimizer, self-play budget, and evaluation fixed. All play and evaluation are searchless. Four fine-tuned conditions share that pipeline—(i) no regularizer; (ii) the entropy bonus; (iii) a reverse-KL anchor to πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}}; and (iv) the forward-KL prior (ours)—and all are measured against the frozen base, the reference to beat. The four are matched on regularization strength and compute. Each arm’s coefficient β⋆\beta^{\star} is selected by overall accuracy on the 10,00010{,}000-puzzle suite described under Metrics below—10−210^{-2} for five of the six term–temperature arms, 10−410^{-4} for the sixth (the entropy bonus without the adaptive temperature)—and every subsequent evaluation uses the selected model (Table 6, Appendix G). Ratings carry 95%95\% confidence intervals (one run per cell; Appendix F); the full training configuration is in Table 2 and Appendix G.

Ablation design.

The runs cross two factors: the exploration term with its coefficient β\beta, and the entropy-adaptive sampling temperature against a fixed τ≡1\tau\equiv 1 baseline, so that the temperature’s contribution is separated from the exploration term’s. For each regularizer we sweep β\beta over the same five-point decade grid from 10−410^{-4} to 11, so that every arm is selected on identical footing (Appendix G lists the full matrix). Fixing the term and varying β\beta locates each method’s best operating point on that suite (Table 6); fixing β\beta and varying the temperature isolates the adaptive temperature; the no-regularizer runs anchor both axes.

Metrics.

Playing strength is reported two ways in Table 1: relative searchless Elo from a closed round-robin, which resolves within-pool differences and reaches an absolute axis only through a single external anchor on the base, and each model’s direct record over 1,0001{,}000 games against the base—its win–draw–loss (W–D–L) record, and the BayesElo likelihood of superiority (LOS) that it is the stronger player. The protocol is in Appendix F.

Tactical accuracy is measured on three suites of Lichess puzzles. The first is the 10,00010{,}000-puzzle suite released by Ruoss et al. (2024) and reported again in the Chessformer evaluation (Monroe et al., 2026); scoring on it keeps our base comparable with the published figure for the same network (Appendix B), and we use it to select each arm’s coefficient (Table 6). Ten thousand puzzles are too few for the comparisons this paper turns on, however: the 95%95\% Wilson interval at that size is ≈±0.45\approx\!\pm 0.45 percentage points, while the fine-tuned arms separate by a few tenths of a point. We therefore built two larger suites, sampling the public Lichess puzzle database the same way: a uniformly sampled 100,000100{,}000-puzzle suite, which tightens the interval to ≈±0.15\approx\!\pm 0.15 points, and a 20,00020{,}000-puzzle suite restricted to puzzles rated ≥2400\geq\!2400, which spends the sample where the base still fails and the arms still differ. Those ratings are Lichess’s Glicko-2 estimates from human solve rates, so they order puzzles by human difficulty rather than by engine depth—a signal regular enough that predicting it from the board is itself a studied task (Miłosz and Kapusta, 2024; Miłosz, 2025). These two carry every headline accuracy in the paper (Table 1).

Exploration versus collapse plays out over sequences, so to tie strength to mechanism we add two sequence-level diagnostics, trajectory coverage and the solution probability, defined next.

Trajectory coverage ΩKN\Omega^{N}_{K}.

From a state ss we draw complete depth-NN trajectories from the policy’s play distribution without replacement: a draw samples a continuation move by move, its trajectory probability πθ​(ξ∣s)=∏t=1Nπθ​(at∣st−1)\pi_{\theta}(\xi\mid s)=\prod_{t=1}^{N}\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t-1}) is recorded, and that mass is removed from the tree and the remainder renormalized (implemented by subtracting the trajectory’s mass along its path), so the next draw samples among the lines not yet seen. The coverage after KK draws,

ΩKN​(s)=𝔼⁡[∑i=1Kπθ​(ξi∣s)],\Omega^{N}_{K}(s)=\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{i=1}^{K}\pi_{\theta}(\xi_{i}\mid s)\Big], (8)

with the expectation over the sampling and each πθ​(ξi∣s)\pi_{\theta}(\xi_{i}\mid s) evaluated under the original policy, is the total mass of the KK distinct lines drawn: a near-deterministic policy reaches ΩKN≈1\Omega^{N}_{K}\approx 1 within a handful of draws, while a policy that spreads mass over many promising continuations needs thousands. Sweeping KK at fixed NN traces a coverage curve whose shape distinguishes collapse from prior-directed spreading, the multi-step counterpart of the single-state coverage and entropy diagnostics; sampled models are drawn through the same play distribution used in self-play (the tempered μ\mu for adaptive-temperature models), so the curve measures how quickly self-play exhausts what the policy will actually play.

Solution probability, via the solution negative log-likelihood (NLL).

Tactics accuracy scores whether the arg​max\argmax move solves a puzzle, which is harsh on a stochastic policy that ranks the solution highly without making it the single most probable move. Each puzzle specifies a ground-truth line ξ⋆=(a1⋆,…,aM⋆)\xi^{\star}=(a^{\star}_{1},\dots,a^{\star}_{M}) visiting positions s0⋆,…,sM−1⋆s^{\star}_{0},\dots,s^{\star}_{M-1}, with a set W⁡(st⋆)W(s^{\star}_{t}) of winning moves at each position (usually the single at+1⋆a^{\star}_{t+1}; where several moves win, all are credited). Per puzzle we compute the solution NLL, the log-mass the policy keeps along the line,

ℓ(ξ⋆)=−∑t=1Mlog∑a∈W⁡(st−1⋆)πθ(a∣st−1⋆),\ell(\xi^{\star})=-\sum_{t=1}^{M}\log\!\!\sum_{a\in W(s^{\star}_{t-1})}\!\!\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s^{\star}_{t-1}), (9)

in nats, and report the solution probability p⋆=e−ℓ⁡(ξ⋆)p^{\star}=e^{-\ell(\xi^{\star})}—the probability of sampling the entire line ξ⋆\xi^{\star} in one rollout (exactly ∏tπθ​(at⋆∣st−1⋆)\prod_{t}\pi_{\theta}(a^{\star}_{t}\mid s^{\star}_{t-1}) when each position admits a single winning move). Aggregation happens in the log domain: averaging ℓ\ell over puzzles and exponentiating yields the geometric-mean solution probability, which we report unless stated otherwise. The geometric mean is the right default for retention because the probability is a product along the line and heavy losses should not be masked: a policy that drives one solution toward zero probability is charged in full, where the arithmetic mean can stay high on the strength of the solutions it keeps (e.g., solution probabilities 0.90.9, 0.8990.899, and 0.0010.001 across three puzzles give an arithmetic mean of 0.6000.600 but a geometric mean of only 0.0930.093)—a divergence between the two means is itself a collapse signal, which Section 3.3 exploits. Paired model comparisons are likewise made in the log domain (per-puzzle NLL differences, reported as probability ratios). We compute ℓ\ell under the untempered πθ\pi_{\theta} (EMA weights), so it measures the learned policy’s intrinsic retention of the solution rather than the tempered behavior policy’s, and it rewards exactly the property prior-directed exploration is meant to preserve: keeping the correct line in support.

3.2  Searchless playing strength

Because the gains are small, we read the ladder and the direct record together. Self-play moves the base, but modestly. The forward-KL prior at fixed temperature tops the ladder at +16.6±8.3+16.6\pm 8.3 Elo over the 23742374 base; head-to-head it outscores the base 0.520.52 over 1,0001{,}000 games (361361–318318–321321 W–D–L, likelihood of superiority 0.940.94)—a real but slender edge, short of decisive. The reverse-KL anchor is tied on the ladder (+16.2±8.3+16.2\pm 8.3) and in fact wins its own match against the base more clearly (0.550.55, LOS >0.99>0.99), so on strength the two prior-anchored directions are indistinguishable and we do not claim the forward direction is the stronger player. We read the ladder cautiously for a second reason: a closed-pool rating and a direct record can diverge—the unregularized fixed-temperature run rates near zero on the ladder yet outscores the base 0.530.53 head-to-head—because the rating reflects play against the whole pool, not the base alone.

Two further cautions apply. The headline is the largest of many swept configurations, so part of its margin is selection (winner’s-curse) inflation the per-row interval does not capture. And the exploration term’s own contribution is modest and temperature-dependent: at fixed temperature the forward-KL prior adds ≈17\approx\!17 Elo over no regularizer (+16.6+16.6 versus −0.5-0.5), but with the adaptive temperature, which alone already reaches +9.8+9.8, it adds only ≈2\approx\!2 (+11.7+11.7 versus +9.8+9.8)—prior and temperature are partly substitutes. What the strength results do establish is the coarse ordering—anchoring exploration to the prior helps and clearly beats the fragile entropy bonus, whose rating is acutely sensitive to its coefficient: without the adaptive temperature it peaks at just +6.6+6.6 Elo (its selected β=10−4\beta=10^{-4}) and falls to −119-119 by β=10−2\beta=10^{-2} and −576-576 at β=1\beta=1 (Table 6 tracks the accompanying accuracy collapse)—while the forward-versus-reverse question turns on move-distribution behavior the Elo cannot see, which Sections 3.3 and 3.4 take up.

3.3  Tactical accuracy, retention, and coverage

With the arms fixed by that selection, we turn from strength to the policies themselves: how tactical accuracy responds to the coefficient, how much probability each policy retains on winning lines, and how concentrated its play becomes.

Coefficient sweep.

To trace the shape of the response rather than merely locate its optimum, we re-evaluate the headline forward-KL-with-adaptive-temperature arm on the 100,000100{,}000-puzzle suite and add four intermediate half-decade points, giving the nine-point curve of Figure 5; these extra points are for resolution only and play no part in selection. The larger suite’s 95%95\% intervals of about ±0.14\pm 0.14 percentage points resolve differences the 10,00010{,}000-puzzle suite could not. The response to β\beta has a clean single minimum. The frozen base errs on 6.15%6.15\% of the puzzles and the unregularized run (β=0\beta=0) on 5.94%5.94\%, so self-play already helps; adding the forward-KL prior helps further, with the error falling to 5.13%5.13\% at β=10−2\beta=10^{-2}, 1.021.02 percentage points below the base and 0.810.81 below the unregularized run—both gaps several intervals wide. The response is U-shaped in log⁡β\log\beta with its trough near β∈[3⋅10−3,3⋅10−2]\beta\in[3\cdot 10^{-3},3\cdot 10^{-2}], set between two limits the sweep approaches without reaching: as β→0\beta\to 0 the objective reverts to the unregularized run (5.94%5.94\%), and as β\beta grows the penalty dominates the reward and pulls the policy back toward the base itself (6.15%6.15\%), which it would recover exactly in the limit. Too small a weight therefore barely restrains collapse and too large a weight over-regularizes: by β=1\beta=1 the error has climbed to 5.91%5.91\%, surrendering the entire margin over the unregularized run on its way to the base. This slice confirms at ten times the scale the operating point β=10−2\beta=10^{-2} selected on the smaller suite (Table 6). We do not over-read it: it varies the forward KL and the adaptive temperature jointly, on a tactics proxy, so it separates the forward-KL direction neither from the adaptive temperature nor from value-head fine-tuning, and does not show that forward KL beats the entropy bonus—a U-shaped response to a coefficient is generic to regularizers.

Accuracy by mate depth.

Table 3 breaks searchless accuracy down by forced-mate depth on the mate-in-11 to 55 suite of Lin et al. (2026). The base solves nearly every short mate and falls off with depth, from 99.9%99.9\% at N=1N\!=\!1 to 58.0%58.0\% at N=5N\!=\!5; fine-tuning leaves the easy mates at ceiling and concentrates its gains on the deeper mates (N≥3N\!\geq\!3), mirroring the ≥2400\geq\!2400 puzzle column of Table 1.

Solution retention.

Argmax accuracy asks only whether the top move is right; a sharper question is what probability the policy retains on the full winning line—the chance of sampling the entire solution in one pass, the quantity prior-directed exploration is meant to protect, and the one that keeps improvement reachable during training (Section 2.1). Table 4 reports the geometric-mean p⋆p^{\star} for the base and the fine-tuned conditions, and Figure 6 (left) plots the two prior-anchored models’ gain over the base by mate depth. The forward prior retains solutions better than the base on every suite; the reverse anchor does too on short and mid-depth lines but falls below the base on the hardest sets (0.1780.178 versus 0.1990.199 on the ≥2400\geq\!2400 puzzles; 0.1260.126 versus 0.1610.161 at mate-in-5). The two directions split exactly as the mechanism predicts. The mode-seeking reverse anchor is sharper where lines are short, its retained probability 11–4%4\% higher (as a ratio) on the full tactics suite and on mates in one to three, while the mass-covering forward prior wins increasingly with difficulty and depth: its solution probability is 33%33\% higher on the ≥2400\geq\!2400 puzzles (paired ratio 1.331.33) and 11%11\% and 34%34\% higher at mate-in-4 and 5. The ≥2400\geq\!2400 subset shows the collapse signature directly, in the two means of Table 4: the reverse anchor’s arithmetic-mean solution probability (0.570.57) tops the forward prior’s (0.530.53) and nearly doubles the base’s (0.300.30), yet its geometric mean falls below even the base’s—it seizes some hard solutions outright while dropping others toward zero probability, where the forward prior keeps nearly all of them in support. The unregularized run is the same failure at its limit: the highest arithmetic mean in the study (0.600.60) against a geometric mean of 0.010.01, a sixty-fold gap. Binned by puzzle rating on the 100,000100{,}000-puzzle suite (Figure 6, right), the comparison crosses over near rating 2,0002{,}000: the reverse anchor is ahead on every easier bin and the forward prior on every harder one, and on the ≥2600\geq\!2600 bin the reverse anchor’s retention collapses well below the base’s (−0.38-0.38 nats) while the forward prior’s stays near it. Argmax accuracy follows the same gradient, with a turn at the top: both prior-anchored models gain under a tenth of a point where the base already saturates below rating 1,0001{,}000, rising to +3.5+3.5 points in the 2,4002{,}400–2,6002{,}600 bin before falling back to +1.8+1.8 on the hardest puzzles, where nearly half the base’s failures stay out of reach.

The entropy bonus makes the third corner of the comparison, and it fails in the opposite way. Its adaptive-temperature model—the strongest arg​max\argmax puzzle-solver among the self-play runs (Table 1)—retains dramatically less of every solution than the base does: 0.2220.222 versus 0.6600.660 on the tactics suite, 0.1030.103 versus 0.1990.199 on its ≥2400\geq\!2400 puzzles, and 0.3990.399 versus 0.9150.915 even at mate-in-1, where its arg​max\argmax accuracy is at ceiling (losses of 0.830.83–2.712.71 nats across the mate depths and 0.530.53–1.341.34 nats across the rating bins). This is not the reverse anchor’s mode-seeking collapse but the uninformed spreading of Section 2.1 made visible: the entropy bonus leaves the top move in place while flattening the distribution around it, so the arg​max\argmax stays right as the mass a training run would need to sample drains away. The three regularizers thus separate cleanly at the distribution level even where arg​max\argmax metrics tie.

Trajectory coverage.

Retention asks about ground-truth lines; the trajectory coverage ΩKN\Omega^{N}_{K} asks how concentrated the policy’s own play is (Section 3.1). We draw depth-44 trajectories from the initial position for every exploration term, in both temperature variants (Figure 7). Covering 95%95\% of the mass—out of 197,281197{,}281 legal depth-44 continuations—takes about 22,00022{,}000 draws for the frozen base (15,00015{,}000 through the tempered μ\mu), 4,1004{,}100 for the entropy bonus, 1,4001{,}400 for the forward-KL prior, and 700700 for the reverse-KL anchor (3,2003{,}200, 1,6001{,}600, and 640640 for their no-temperature counterparts); the unregularized run needs exactly one in both variants, a single opening line carrying 99.9%99.9\% of its mass—the self-sealing collapse of Section 2.1 realized in full, and the sequence-level face of its retention profile in Table 4. Every regularizer prevents that collapse, and the survivors order exactly as the mechanism predicts: the mode-seeking anchor concentrates about twice as hard as the mass-covering prior, which in turn stays well inside the entropy bonus’s near-uniform spread. All fine-tuned policies are far more concentrated than the base—the expected effect of the reward sharpening within the prior’s support—so the diagnostic separates the exploration terms from one another, not fine-tuning from its absence. The measurement is at a single position and depth; Appendix H repeats it at three further opening tabiyas of different character, where the central ordering—reverse anchor tightest, forward prior wider, base widest by more than an order of magnitude, the unregularized run collapsed—reproduces at each (Figure 10).

3.4  Policy shape: concentration, coverage, and sampled play

The trajectory-coverage diagnostic of Section 3.3 measures how concentrated each policy’s play is; here we tie that concentration to strength and add three single-state diagnostics of the policies themselves. We run a second closed round-robin over the ten configurations of Figure 10 in Appendix H—the frozen base sampled raw and through the tempered μ\mu, and each exploration term at both temperatures—in which every model samples its move rather than taking the arg​max\argmax, playing through the behavior policy it used in self-play (Equation (6); a τ≡1\tau\!\equiv\!1 arm plays its raw πθ\pi_{\theta}). Alongside the resulting ratings, Table 5 reports three diagnostics of the policy each model actually plays: its move-distribution entropy, its two KL divergences to the raw base, and how much of its mass stays on the base’s top moves.

Under sampling, strength becomes a read-out of concentration. The ratings span ≈670\approx\!670 Elo, more than twenty times the arg​max\argmax ladder’s ≈30\approx\!30 (Table 1), and they track move entropy inversely: the more a policy concentrates, the better it plays when its moves are sampled, because a diffuse policy squanders draws on its low-probability tail. This is a diagnostic of the policies’ shape, not a second measure of playing skill—the arg​max\argmax ladder is the strength result, and the sampled ordering (in which the reverse arm edges the forward by a margin the arg​max\argmax ladder does not show, tracking its slightly harder concentration in Figure 10) merely re-scores how sharp each policy is. The adaptive temperature is visible directly: tempering the base lifts it +361+361 Elo by sharpening its play (H\Ent from 1.691.69 to 0.390.39), and every adaptive arm outranks its τ≡1\tau\!\equiv\!1 twin.

The forward and reverse KL confirm the mechanism on played positions. Reading the τ≡1\tau\!\equiv\!1 rows, whose eval policy is the raw learned πθ\pi_{\theta} and whose divergence to the base is therefore comparable across arms, the forward-KL prior keeps DKL(πbase∥πθ)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\theta}\right) lowest (0.220.22), the reverse anchor higher (0.600.60), and the entropy bonus higher still (1.261.26)—the mass-covering penalty covers the base’s mass two-to-six times more faithfully than the alternatives, the zero-avoiding asymmetry of Figure 2 measured rather than argued. The tempered-μ\mu rows carry a much larger forward KL (up to 1111) because tempering drives μ\mu toward zero off the top moves, which the base cannot cover—a property of the tempered behavior policy, not of the learned πθ\pi_{\theta}.

3.5  What fine-tuning recovers

The two prior-anchored models newly solve 1,4051{,}405 and 1,3781{,}378 puzzles the base fails (and give back 383383 and 398398, for the net gains of Table 1), and the retention machinery above predicts which: improvement must be sampled before it can be reinforced (Section 2.1), so the failures fine-tuning can fix should be exactly those whose solution the base still plays with non-negligible probability. That is what we find (Figure 8). The policy is Markovian, so we score recovery at the level of positions, under the multi-solution ground truth of Table 1 (a move is correct if it is an optimal mate or the marked move): on the 100,000100{,}000-puzzle suite the base plays a wrong move at 6,8406{,}840 of its 231,739231{,}739 solver positions, and a position counts as recovered when the fine-tuned model’s move there is correct—the forward prior recovers 1,5951{,}595 of them, the reverse anchor 1,5601{,}560. Binned by the probability the base retains on the solution at the position, recovery is gated: neither model recovers any of the 390390 positions with πbase​(solution)<0.05\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\text{solution})<0.05, they recover about 4%4\% of the 1,3451{,}345 in [0.05,0.15)[0.05,0.15), 2121–22%22\% of the 2,8972{,}897 in [0.15,0.3)[0.15,0.3), and about 41%41\% of the 2,2082{,}208 above 0.30.3 (geometric-mean retention of 0.300.30/0.310.31 at recovered positions versus 0.170.17 at unrecovered). The rank view says the same thing more sharply: at 71%71\% of the base’s wrong positions the solution is ranked second, and these recover at 29%29\%, falling to 11%11\% at rank 33 and about 5%5\% at ranks 44–55; none of the 186186 positions with the solution at rank 66 or deeper is recovered by either model, and the deepest recovered solution sat at rank 55. The gap that had to be closed is correspondingly narrow: at recovered positions the base’s top move led the solution by a median of 6.56.5 percentage points, against 2424 points at the positions that stay wrong. Fine-tuning, under either anchor, is near-miss promotion: it reorders the top of the distribution the prior kept alive, and it never resurrects a move the base had effectively discarded. Recovery, where it happens, is decisive: the fine-tuned policies place a mean 3636/4242 additional percentage points of mass on the recovered solutions (medians 3535/4343), and the puzzles gained are hard ones—mean rating 2,0282{,}028/2,0202{,}020, far above the base’s solved set (1,4291{,}429) though below its average failure (2,1902{,}190), as the retention gate predicts. The give-backs are the same trade in reverse, still near misses (on 93%93\%/92%92\% the solution remains at rank 22 of the fine-tuned output) and shallow—the probability leaked off those solutions has median 5.85.8/7.77.7 points, against the 3636/4242-point surges of the recoveries. Give-back is gated from above as recovery is gated from below: of the more than 200,000200{,}000 positions where the base’s top move leads the runner-up by over 0.60.6, neither model gives back a single one. Losing a puzzle is an arg​max\argmax flip between two close moves; gaining one is a commitment. The value head moves with the policy: at recovered positions the base’s win-minus-loss estimate has median 0.020.02—the value head barely sees the win it is failing to play—and fine-tuning lifts it to 0.080.08/0.100.10, while at unrecovered positions, where the base already reads the position more clearly (0.180.18), it changes little (0.170.17/0.190.19).

Where the two anchors differ.

The two anchors recover a large shared core and a small distinct fringe—1,1981{,}198 puzzles both fix, plus 207207 exclusive to the forward prior and 180180 to the reverse anchor—and the fringes differ in kind. The forward prior’s exclusive recoveries reach lower into the retained tail and are the harder puzzles: median base solution probability 0.2850.285 and mean rating 2,1392{,}139, against the reverse anchor’s 0.2970.297 and 2,0992{,}099. This is the per-puzzle face of the retention split of Table 4: the mass-covering prior holds probability on hard, deep solutions that the mode-seeking anchor lets go, and those are the wins only it can then promote. Appendix H walks through three exclusive recoveries of each anchor (Figure 9), annotating every candidate move with the base’s own value-head verdict and a Stockfish oracle; in five of the six positions the base’s value head already separates the winning move from the played one, so the first time self-play samples the retained move, the advantage signal is immediate.

3.6  Tactical accuracy versus playing strength

That any single evaluation figure is an imperfect proxy for playing strength is itself known—a searchless transformer’s rating swings some 600600 points between the human and engine pools it is measured in (Ruoss et al., 2024), and the imitation-versus-strength split is the premise of McIlroy-Young et al. (2020)—but our matched-compute sweep lets us quantify how wide the tactics-versus-strength gap is here, and it is wide. Across the eight fine-tuned configurations of Table 1 the two axes move independently: every one that improves overall accuracy does so within a narrow band (+0.15+0.15 to +1.05+1.05 percentage points) while ratings range from −5.8-5.8 to +16.6+16.6 Elo and straddle the base. The clearest case among the self-play runs is the entropy bonus with adaptive temperature, which posts the highest overall puzzle accuracy of any of them (94.90%94.90\%, +1.05+1.05 percentage points) yet earns no playing strength: its rating (−5.8-5.8 Elo) is statistically indistinguishable from the base, its interval spanning zero and its head-to-head score 0.490.49. Pushed harder the split turns to caricature: an entropy coefficient of 11 still answers 83.1%83.1\% of the 10,00010{,}000-puzzle suite correctly (Table 6) while losing 933933 of its 1,0001{,}000 games to the base.

Starker still is a control that optimizes puzzles directly: fine-tuning the same base for the same 2,0002{,}000 steps by supervised learning on the puzzle solutions rather than by self-play RL (Table 1, last row). Its training pool is drawn from the Lichess puzzle database with both evaluation suites removed, so it is scored on positions it has never seen. It posts by far the largest tactical gains in the study—overall accuracy →96.80%93.85\!\to\!96.80\% (+2.95+2.95 percentage points) and on the ≥2400\geq\!2400 suite →67.95%60.01\!\to\!67.95\% (+7.94+7.94 percentage points), around three times the largest gain from any RL condition—yet its searchless rating collapses to −258.0±9.1-258.0\pm 9.1 Elo, roughly a one-in-five score against the base. The cause is the state-distribution mismatch of Section 1, here induced on purpose: supervising on a fixed external set of positions rather than on states from the policy’s own play sharpens move-by-move tactics while whole-game strength falls apart. The lesson is not that puzzle accuracy is a bad measure—it is the direct measure of the tactical skill we target, and the dense, cheap signal our coefficient sweeps rely on—but that it measures a different capability than playing strength: most fine-tuning recipes lift tactics, while strength is what separates a prior-anchored run that gains a little from an entropy run that does not gain at all and a puzzle-tuned control that collapses. An evaluation must therefore carry both axes separately. The forward- and reverse-KL priors are the configurations that hold both up at once, raising tactical accuracy while keeping strength at or above the base, and that coupling—not the puzzle figure on its own—is the result that bears on searchless play.

4  Related Work

Searchless chess.

Classical neural engines couple a network with a large test-time search; a recent line almost removes it, its strongest members playing at human master level. Ruoss et al. (2024) distill Stockfish action-values into a transformer used as a depth-one move selector, one forward pass per legal child with no recursion; DiffuSearch folds an implicit search into a discrete-diffusion policy (Ye et al., 2025); Hamara et al. (2025) navigate a contrastively learned value embedding; and the Chessformer architecture (Monroe et al., 2026) as trained by Lc0 (The LCZero Authors, 2018), our base and, in engine-versus-engine play, the strongest of these, selects each move from a single forward pass of its policy head. A related thread interprets how such networks compute without explicit search (Jenner et al., 2024; Sandmann et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026), and a separate imitation line fits human move distributions for human-like play rather than maximal strength (McIlroy-Young et al., 2020); a further human-centric line predicts how hard a position is for people, regressing Lichess’s Glicko-2 puzzle ratings from the board (Miłosz and Kapusta, 2024; Miłosz, 2025). The playing systems in this line are obtained by imitation and then frozen.

RL for games and pretrained policies.

AlphaZero learns strong policies by self-play guided by MCTS (Silver et al., 2018), extended by MuZero to planning with a learned model (Schrittwieser et al., 2020), and Lc0 trains openly available networks of this kind (The LCZero Authors, 2018; Monroe et al., 2026). That self-play loop produces the search-trained network we start from; it does not optimize the network’s own searchless play. Separately, RL adapts strong pretrained policies, as in RLHF and RLVR, which fine-tune language models against a reward with a KL anchor to the base (Ouyang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024). We join the two: we take an externally strong searchless network and fine-tune it by self-play RL whose objective is searchless strength itself, neither proposing a new way to obtain the network nor merely anchoring it to its initialization.

Exploration regularizers, and the three roles of the KL.

An entropy bonus is the standard way to maintain exploration and avoid deterministic collapse (Williams and Peng, 1991; Mnih et al., 2016; Schulman et al., 2017), promoted to part of the objective in maximum-entropy RL (Haarnoja et al., 2018). Intrinsic-reward methods drive exploration with novelty signals, count-based bonuses (Bellemare et al., 2016), prediction-error curiosity (Pathak et al., 2017), and random network distillation (Burda et al., 2019), which modify the reward rather than the action-distribution regularizer and are orthogonal to what we study. A closer neighbor is GFlowNets’ mass-covering objective of sampling in proportion to reward (Bengio et al., 2021), which pursues the same anti-collapse, multi-modal coverage we seek but enforces it by flow-matching rather than a divergence penalty. Entropy collapse is now a central concern in language-model post-training (Cui et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). GX-Chen et al. (2025) qualify the direction argument we rely on: under KL-regularized RL the direction fixes only the family of optimal distributions, with mode coverage governed mainly by the regularization strength and the scale of rewards relative to reference probabilities—which is why we select β\beta empirically and rest the forward-versus-reverse case on the measured coverage of Section 3.3 rather than on direction alone. The KL itself plays three distinct roles in policy optimization: it constrains each update to the previous policy as a trust region (Kakade, 2002; Schulman et al., 2015; Schulman et al., 2017); it regularizes toward a fixed reference or learned default, generalizing maximum-entropy RL (Galashov et al., 2019; Tirumala et al., 2022), underpinning control-as-inference (Levine, 2018) and maximum a posteriori policy optimisation (MPO) (Abdolmaleki et al., 2018), and anchoring fine-tuned models in RLHF and RLVR (Ouyang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024); and, in our use, it drives exploration. Closest to our setting, Ota et al. (2026) combine the first two roles for two-player zero-sum games—a reverse KL to the current iterate together with an entropy bonus—prove local convergence, and evaluate on five board games including a reduced chess; their agents learn from scratch by self-play, where we adapt an externally strong released network, and their entropy term points at the uniform distribution where ours points at that network. The fixed-reference role is conventionally taken in the policy-first, mode-seeking direction DKL(πθ∥π0)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}\,\big\|\,\pi_{0}\right), to keep the policy near its reference; the trust-region role is taken in either direction, reference-first in trust region policy optimization (TRPO) and PPO’s KL-penalty variant and policy-first in Ota et al. (2026). The exploration regularizers above all point at the uniform distribution. We keep the reference-policy regularizer, reverse its direction, and swap its reference for a fixed, externally strong, search-derived prior.

Forward-KL regularization, and the closest work.

Forward, mass-covering KL toward a reference is well established, but toward ends other than exploration. Label smoothing adds a forward KL to the uniform distribution (Szegedy et al., 2016; Pereyra et al., 2017); toward a strong reference, ff-DPO generalizes direct preference optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023) to ff-divergences including the forward KL (Wang et al., 2024), and knowledge distillation matches a teacher under the forward KL (Hinton et al., 2015), which on-policy distillation generalizes to a family of divergences scored on student-generated data (Agarwal et al., 2024). In all of these the divergence serves regularization, alignment, or distillation, not exploration. Closest to us, two recent language-model works turn the forward direction toward exploration: diversity-preserving hybrid RL (DPH-RL) anchors mass-covering ff-divergences to the model’s own initial policy as a rehearsal term against diversity collapse (Li et al., 2025), and rewards-aware policy optimization (RAPO) replaces the reverse-KL anchor with a forward KL to explore beyond the base model’s support, adding a reward-aware reweighting of the reference to steer exploration within it (Deng et al., 2025). We differ on three points. We replace the entropy bonus, casting prior-directed exploration as a generalization of entropy regularization rather than a variant of the trust-region anchor. Our reference is a fixed, externally strong, search-derived prior used as is to cover its already-informed support, not the model’s own initial policy or a reference reweighted to redirect exploration. And our domain is searchless chess, where the target is playing strength rather than reasoning accuracy.

5  Conclusion

Searchless chess networks are trained to imitate a search and then deployed without one. We argued that self-play RL is the natural way to close this gap, optimizing single-pass strength directly, and that the exploration it needs is better served by the network’s own search-derived prior than by an entropy bonus: replacing the bonus with a forward, mass-covering KL toward the MCTS visit-count prior drives the policy to cover exactly the moves the prior judges promising, avoiding both uninformed spreading and mode collapse, while the reward sharpens within that support. In about two thousand steps, far below the search that produced the network, this delivers a clear tactical improvement—higher puzzle accuracy and deeper forced mates—while searchless playing strength holds at or just above the base, the forward-KL prior topping the rating ladder with the reverse-KL anchor statistically tied.

The finding we underline constrains how such fine-tuning should be read: tactical accuracy and playing strength dissociate, so a method that lifts puzzle accuracy is not thereby a stronger player, and the worth of anchoring exploration to the prior is that it improves tactics without spending strength. The distribution-level measurements separate the two anchoring directions as the mechanism predicts—the mode-seeking anchor concentrates about twice as hard and drops the hardest solutions, where the mass-covering prior keeps them, and without any regularizer self-play collapses onto a single line of play—while the per-puzzle recovery analysis says what fine-tuning can and cannot fix: it promotes the near misses the prior kept alive and never resurrects a move the base had discarded, which is why keeping candidates sampled is the exploration term’s whole job.

Chess is a clean testbed because its search-derived priors are unusually strong. The recipe should extend to settings that share its two enabling conditions, an enumerable per-state reference and an exploratory prior worth covering, most naturally other games and combinatorial planning with a search- or ensemble-derived prior. The standard language-model setting is not excluded in principle but meets the enumerability condition only at a cost: the forward KL needs the reference’s full next-token distribution, the O⁡(|V|)O(|V|) teacher pass that on-policy distillation already pays (Agarwal et al., 2024) but that is dear to add on top of RL exploration (Section 2.2)—so chess serves here to exhibit the mechanism where the prior is cheap and strong, not to rule language out.

Limitations.

Our claims are scoped to one domain and one base network. The forward-versus-reverse evidence supports the mechanism on both retention and coverage, but the two directions remain tied on strength, and the strength gains are small in absolute terms—a reminder that two thousand steps of fine-tuning adjust the base network rather than remake it.

The method carries two structural requirements. The forward KL is computed exactly only for a categorical distribution over a modest action set; large action spaces require estimation, the cost that makes the reverse direction the default there. And it helps only when the prior’s support is worth covering: a weak or biased prior would be faithfully covered, so annealing β\beta or combining references is a natural extension. Neither evaluation axis is a reliable arbiter alone either—self-play Elo can flatter a pool with shared blind spots, and tactical accuracy can rise even for a weaker player—so we claim improvements only where both agree.

Two risks are specific to the self-play recipe. Because terminated games restart from the standard initial position, a low-temperature, prior-anchored policy could narrow opening diversity over training; persistent root randomization, as in AlphaZero, is the natural safeguard. Figure 7 quantifies the narrowing after training—real for every run but far from collapse under any regularizer—though it measures the policy’s play distribution, not the opening diversity of the games actually generated. And the frozen prior is least reliable on exactly the off-distribution states self-play reaches, where forcing coverage of its support is least justified—the covariate shift reappearing one level up—which annealing β\beta as the policy drifts would mitigate.
