Appendix A Notation, MDP, and networks

We model chess as an episodic, two-player, zero-sum Markov decision process. A state ss comprises the board, the side to move, and the auxiliary rule information (castling rights, en-passant target, repetition history). The agent selects a legal move a∈𝒜⁡(s)a\in\mathcal{A}(s); dynamics are deterministic, s′=T⁡(s,a)s^{\prime}=T(s,a). Episodes end by the laws of chess with an outcome in {win,draw,loss}\{\text{win},\text{draw},\text{loss}\} from the mover’s view; intermediate rewards are zero and the discount is γ=1\gamma=1, so an episode’s return is its terminal score.

The network has a shared trunk θ\theta and two heads. The policy head defines πθ(⋅∣s)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s) over 𝒜⁡(s)\mathcal{A}(s). The value head outputs a categorical WDL distribution 𝐩θ​(s)=(pθW​(s),pθD​(s),pθL​(s))\mathbf{p}_{\theta}(s)=(p^{\mathrm{W}}_{\theta}(s),p^{\mathrm{D}}_{\theta}(s),p^{\mathrm{L}}_{\theta}(s)) from the mover’s view, giving the scalar score

vθ​(s)=pθW​(s)+12​pθD​(s)∈[0,1]v_{\theta}(s)=p^{\mathrm{W}}_{\theta}(s)+\tfrac{1}{2}\,p^{\mathrm{D}}_{\theta}(s)\in[0,1] (10)

(note that we assume the standard 1-0.5-0 scoring, though alternative rules rewarding decisive games, such as the 3-1-0 football-style system historically applied in events like the Bilbao Chess Masters, are sometimes used to discourage quick draws).

After a move the opponent is to move, so the mover’s score is 1−v⁡(s′)1-v(s^{\prime}), with WDL vector obtained by swapping the win and loss components, flip⁡(𝐩)=(pL,pD,pW)\operatorname{flip}(\mathbf{p})=(p^{\mathrm{L}},p^{\mathrm{D}},p^{\mathrm{W}}). We keep three copies of the network. The online model πθ\pi_{\theta} is the only one updated by gradient descent and is initialized from the reference. The reference πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}}, the frozen Chessformer, is the target of the forward-KL penalty. An EMA model θ¯\bar{\theta} tracks the online weights,

θ¯←α​θ¯+(1−α)​θ,α∈(0,1),\bar{\theta}\leftarrow\alpha\,\bar{\theta}+(1-\alpha)\,\theta,\qquad\alpha\in(0,1), (11)

serving as a slowly-moving target as in deep Q-learning (Mnih et al., 2015); decoupling bootstrap targets from the rapidly changing online parameters is what stabilizes value learning.

Appendix B Base network: Chessformer

The network we fine-tune is the Chessformer architecture (Monroe et al., 2026) in the instantiation trained and released by Leela Chess Zero (The LCZero Authors, 2018); every run uses the checkpoint BT4-1024x15x32h-swa-6147500 named in Section 3, a 1515-layer encoder-only transformer with 10241024-dimensional embeddings, 3232 attention heads, and a multi-layer-perceptron (MLP) width of 15361536. It matches the 191191M-parameter Leela-CF model of Monroe et al. (2026) in every dimension that work reports, and in accuracy on the 10,00010{,}000-puzzle suite the two share (93.5%93.5\%; Table 6), which is what licenses us to read that work’s rating as this checkpoint’s (Appendix F). A position is presented as 6464 tokens, one per board square, each a depth-112112 feature vector encoding the current and past 77 board positions (piece occupancies, repetition flags, castling rights, side to move, and the halfmove clock). Self-attention is augmented not by a generic positional encoding but by Geometric Attention Bias (GAB), the architecture’s dynamic position encoding: from a compressed representation of the board it generates per-head additive biases over the 64×6464\times 64 square pairs, added to the dot-product logits before the softmax, so that attention adapts to the geometry of the position (Monroe et al., 2026); the Lc0 codebase calls the same module smolgen. The policy head is attention-based—source and destination square representations are multiplied along the embedding axis to form a 64×6464\times 64 matrix of move logits, which restricted to the legal moves gives πθ(⋅∣s)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)—and the value head mean-pools the trunk to predict the win/draw/loss categorical 𝐩θ​(s)\mathbf{p}_{\theta}(s), summarized by the scalar score vθ​(s)v_{\theta}(s) of Appendix A.

The interpretability results we draw on in Section 1 are obtained on a different, smaller Lc0 transformer of the same square-token lineage—the 768768-dimensional, 2424-head T82-768x15x24h network (≈109\approx\!109M parameters) (Sandmann et al., 2025)—not on the checkpoint we fine-tune. It nonetheless shares the encoder-only, 6464-square-token form, a 1515-layer residual stream, and the generated attention-bias module described above with our network, so the layerwise behavior it reports—a strong move identified in intermediate layers and then demoted by the output—is most naturally read as a property of these deep square-token policies rather than of the exact weights we adapt.

The released network is obtained by supervised distillation, not by an online reinforcement-learning loop: its policy head is fit by cross-entropy to the Monte Carlo Tree Search visit-count distributions of AlphaZero-style self-play, and its value head to the win/draw/loss game outcomes (Silver et al., 2018). The data originate from self-play with search, but the network itself only imitates the recorded search statistics, and it is not distilled from a classical engine’s action values—the distinction from the line of Ruoss et al. (2024). This supervised, search-derived origin is what makes the single-pass policy both the noisy pointwise imitation target we move beyond and, as Appendix C argues, an exploratory prior whose support is worth covering.

Appendix C Why the base network’s prior is exploratory

Prior-directed exploration helps only if the reference πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} spreads probability over several promising moves rather than concentrating on one (Section 2.2). This appendix explains why the base network meets that condition by construction. The point to keep in view is that πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} is not an MCTS search performed at play time but the trained network’s single-pass policy, fit during pretraining to imitate the visit-count distributions of such a search. The argument has two steps: those visit-count distributions are exploratory by construction, and the supervised objective that produced the network is mass-covering, so the network inherits their breadth.

Step 1: MCTS visit counts are exploratory by construction.

AlphaZero-style training generates its data with MCTS (Silver et al., 2018). From a position ss the search repeatedly descends the tree, at each node taking the action that maximizes a PUCT score that adds an exploration bonus to the running value estimate,

arg​maxa⁡Q​(s,a)+cpuct​P​(s,a)​∑bN⁡(s,b)1+N⁡(s,a),\argmax_{a}\;Q(s,a)+c_{\mathrm{puct}}\,P(s,a)\,\frac{\sqrt{\textstyle\sum_{b}N(s,b)}}{1+N(s,a)},

so a move with appreciable prior P⁡(s,a)P(s,a) keeps being tried even after another currently looks best, until its visit count N⁡(s,a)N(s,a) catches up. The policy the search exports is not its single best move but the (optionally tempered) visit-count distribution πmcts​(a∣s)∝N​(s,a)1/τ\pi_{\mathrm{mcts}}(a\mid s)\propto N(s,a)^{1/\tau}. Because the bonus spreads visits across every move with non-negligible prior and value, this distribution keeps mass on several moves wherever more than one is reasonable and sharpens only when the search is itself confident, as in forced or clearly decided positions. Visit counts are thus high-entropy exactly where exploration matters and low-entropy where it does not. The argument does not hinge on the specific search variant: more recent Lc0 training can use Gumbel-MuZero (Danihelka et al., 2022), which selects root actions by sampling without replacement rather than by the visit counts above but still returns an improved policy over several root moves. Step 2 needs only that the exported target keep mass on more than one move where more than one is reasonable, which the released network’s policy does.

Step 2: distillation is mass-covering, so the network inherits the spread.

The base network is not the search but a network trained to imitate it: its policy head is fit to the visit-count targets by cross-entropy, which decomposes as

−∑aπmcts(a∣s)logπbase(a∣s)=H(πmcts(⋅∣s))+DKL(πmcts(⋅∣s)∥πbase(⋅∣s)),-\sum_{a}\pi_{\mathrm{mcts}}(a\mid s)\,\log\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(a\mid s)=\Ent\!\big(\pi_{\mathrm{mcts}}(\cdot\mid s)\big)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\mathrm{mcts}}(\cdot\mid s)\,\big\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\cdot\mid s)\right),

that is, up to the target’s own entropy, the forward KL from the visit-count distribution to the network. Forward KL is mass-covering (Section 2.2, Figure 2): it penalizes dropping any move the search visited. A network that collapsed onto one move would pay a large cross-entropy on every position where the search spread its visits, so training transfers the breadth of the visit-count distributions onto the network’s single-pass policy. The mechanism is the one our method re-uses: the network was produced by a forward KL toward exploratory MCTS targets, and we fine-tune it with a forward KL toward the network’s own resulting policy.

Consequence.

The released network’s single-pass policy πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}}, our frozen reference, is therefore exploratory by construction: it carries forward the multi-move spread of the visit counts it was distilled from and sharpens only where the search was decisive. The enabling condition of Section 2.2 holds for this base network without any tuning on our part, so the forward-KL penalty has genuine, search-derived breadth to cover. At the opening position, for instance, the released network keeps its probability spread across several first moves rather than committing to one. A near-deterministic expert, such as a policy distilled from a single oracle move per position, would offer no such breadth, and prior-directed exploration would then collapse toward that one move.

Appendix D Self-play data generation

Data are generated by running NN games in parallel and advancing each by one ply per training iteration. At the start of training only, each slot is seeded with a random opening: we draw k∼Uniform​{0,1,…,60}k\sim\mathrm{Uniform}\{0,1,\dots,60\} and play the first kk full moves by sampling from πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} (tempered by Equation (6) in the adaptive-temperature arms). This one-time randomization staggers the games so the batch spans all phases of play. Thereafter a terminated game restarts from the standard initial position, so that every restarted game is played by the agent from the first move and the data reflect the agent’s own state distribution rather than base-sampled openings; because games end at different times, the batch stays phase-diverse on its own. Each iteration forms a batch of one position per active game. At state ss we query the reference for πbase(⋅∣s)\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\cdot\mid s), the online model for πθ(⋅∣s)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s) and vθ​(s)v_{\theta}(s), and sample the played move from μ(⋅∣s)\mu(\cdot\mid s) of Equation (6). Applying it gives s′=T⁡(s,a)s^{\prime}=T(s,a), which the EMA model evaluates for the bootstrap value vθ¯​(s′)v_{\bar{\theta}}(s^{\prime}) (the true one-hot result when s′s^{\prime} is terminal). One gradient step is then taken, so every transition is used once while fresh.

Appendix E Importance sampling, advantage, and the single-step update

Truncated importance sampling.

Because moves are drawn from the tempered μ\mu rather than from πθ\pi_{\theta}, the transitions are off-policy with respect to the optimized policy. We correct this with a per-sample weight

ρ⁡(s,a)=min⁡(1,πθ​(a∣s)μ⁡(a∣s)),\rho(s,a)=\min\!\Big(1,\ \tfrac{\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}{\mu(a\mid s)}\Big), (12)

treated as a stop-gradient constant and applied to both the policy gradient and the value loss. It corrects only the temperature-induced gap between μ\mu and πθ\pi_{\theta}; with one update per fresh batch there is no policy staleness. Truncating at 11 follows the V-trace estimator of the importance weighted actor-learner architecture (IMPALA) (Espeholt et al., 2018): the sharpened μ\mu oversamples high-probability moves, which receive ρ<1\rho<1, while rarely sampled moves would otherwise carry large weights, and the cap bounds their variance at the cost of a controlled bias. That bias sits exactly where μ\mu sharpens most: in a near-decided position an off-argmax sample has πθ/μ≫1\pi_{\theta}/\mu\gg 1 and is capped to 11, but the advantage there is itself near zero—the successor’s WDL barely moves from the mover’s view—so the uncorrected mass carries almost no gradient. The truncation also reinforces the temperature’s intent: near-decided positions, where μ\mu is sharp, are down-weighted to ρ<1\rho<1 and terminate quickly, leaving the update concentrated where μ≈πθ\mu\approx\pi_{\theta} and the advantage is informative.

Advantage and no normalization.

The one-step TD advantage of Equation (4) pairs the EMA-evaluated successor value, flipped to the mover’s view, with the online estimate at ss. TD(0) (Sutton, 1988) suits this setting because the reference value head is already accurate, so a single bootstrap gives a low-variance, low-bias target. We apply no advantage normalization, separating the two normalizations usually bundled together. Mean-centering: the value loss regresses vθ​(s)v_{\theta}(s) toward the same bootstrapped target that enters AA, and the head starts near-consistent, so over the symmetric self-play population 𝔼⁡[A]≈0\mathbb{E}[A]\approx 0 and a global baseline is near zero. This is an unconditional statement that need not hold per batch or in transients, where the EMA lag and any value-head miscalibration give the one-step residual a systematic sign; we therefore omit per-batch mean-centering as a cheap option rather than rule it out. Std-scaling: dividing by a running standard deviation would rescale the natural units of the advantage, a difference of win probabilities in [−1,1][-1,1], inflating the signal in quiet, low-variance positions relative to sharp ones and injecting a position-dependent bias, so we deliberately avoid it.

Single-step reduction of PPO.

We take one gradient step per fresh batch, which lets us drop the clipping that defines PPO (Schulman et al., 2017). The clipped surrogate is

ℒPPO​(θ)=𝔼(s,a)​[min⁡(r⁡(θ)​A^,clip⁡(r⁡(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)​A^)],r⁡(θ)=πθ​(a∣s)πθold​(a∣s),\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{PPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(s,a)}\!\left[\min\!\big(r(\theta)\hat{A},\ \clip(r(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat{A}\big)\right],\quad r(\theta)=\tfrac{\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a\mid s)}, (13)

with A^​(s,a)=ρ⁡(s,a)​A​(s,a)\hat{A}(s,a)=\rho(s,a)A(s,a). The ratio rr is measured against the policy πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} that collected the data, and the clip enforces a trust region (Schulman et al., 2015) only when rollouts are reused over several epochs, during which πθ\pi_{\theta} drifts from πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}. With a single update there is no reuse: collection and differentiation parameters coincide, r⁡(θ)≡1r(\theta)\equiv 1, the two branches of the minimum are identical, and the clip never activates. The surrogate reduces to the advantage-weighted policy gradient

ℒPG​(θ)=𝔼(s,a)​[ρ⁡(s,a)​A​(s,a)​log⁡πθ​(a∣s)],\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{PG}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(s,a)}\!\left[\rho(s,a)A(s,a)\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\right], (14)

with ρ\rho and AA fixed, matching the single-update-per-batch practice of group relative policy optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024); the truncated weight is still required because μ\mu differs from πθ\pi_{\theta} through the temperature, only the trust-region clip is dropped; a variance-control device thus survives, on the sampling ratio πθ/μ\pi_{\theta}/\mu rather than the temporal ratio rr, which never leaves 11. Dropping it removes the only explicit step-size constraint, so the per-step change in πθ\pi_{\theta} is governed by the (small, layerwise) learning rate rather than by a ratio bound—the EMA target smooths the value estimates that feed AA but does not bound the policy step—the same trade GRPO-style single-epoch updates make; we treat the single step as a simplification, not a stability guarantee in itself.

Value learning and the enumerability remark.

The value head regresses its WDL prediction at ss onto the point-of-view-flipped EMA target 𝐩^​(s)=flip⁡(𝐩θ¯​(s′))\hat{\mathbf{p}}(s)=\operatorname{flip}(\mathbf{p}_{\bar{\theta}}(s^{\prime})) (the one-hot result at terminal s′s^{\prime}) by cross-entropy,

ℒV​(θ)=−𝔼(s,a)​[∑o∈{W,D,L}p^o​(s)​log⁡pθo​(s)],\mathcal{L}_{V}(\theta)=-\,\mathbb{E}_{(s,a)}\!\Big[\textstyle\sum_{o\in\{\mathrm{W},\mathrm{D},\mathrm{L}\}}\hat{p}^{\,o}(s)\log p^{o}_{\theta}(s)\Big], (15)

also weighted by ρ⁡(s,a)\rho(s,a). This ρ\rho-weighting is what makes the regression target on-policy. The value vθ​(s)v_{\theta}(s) should be the one-step value of ss under the online policy, 𝔼a∼πθ​[ 1−vθ¯​(s′)]\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}}[\,1-v_{\bar{\theta}}(s^{\prime})\,], since that is the baseline subtracted in the advantage of Equation (4). Because moves are drawn from the tempered μ\mu, the unweighted target 1−vθ¯​(s′)1-v_{\bar{\theta}}(s^{\prime}) averages to the child value under μ\mu; weighting by ρ⁡(s,a)=min⁡(1,πθ/μ)\rho(s,a)=\min(1,\pi_{\theta}/\mu) corrects the action over which the target is taken, so in expectation the regression targets the πθ\pi_{\theta}-value instead. The action-independence of vθ​(s)v_{\theta}(s) does not reduce this to a state reweighting: the target flip⁡(𝐩θ¯​(s′))\operatorname{flip}(\mathbf{p}_{\bar{\theta}}(s^{\prime})) depends on the sampled move through s′s^{\prime}, and ρ\rho corrects which child it averages over. As on the policy gradient, the truncation at 11 leaves the usual V-trace bias (its fixed point sits between the μ\mu- and πθ\pi_{\theta}-values for under-sampled, high-ratio moves), and the single-step weight corrects the immediate child expectation but not the state-visitation distribution—appropriate for a baseline fit on the states self-play visits. The forward KL, finally, enters as an explicit penalty on the policy loss (as the entropy bonus it replaces would), not as part of the return, so the critic estimates the reward-value of the current policy—the consistent baseline—rather than a max-entropy-style soft value. Finally, on the cost of the forward penalty: the reverse KL DKL(πθ∥πbase)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\right) is an expectation under πθ\pi_{\theta}, estimated for free along the policy’s own rollouts from the reference’s log-probability of each realized action (Schulman, 2020), whereas the forward KL DKL(πbase∥πθ)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\theta}\right) needs the reference’s full distribution at each state. For a language model the exact sum runs over the vocabulary at every token; the sampled alternatives—drawing from the reference offline (Li et al., 2025) or importance-reweighting the policy’s own rollouts (Deng et al., 2025)—avoid it, but the importance weights πbase/πθ\pi_{\mathrm{base}}/\pi_{\theta} are unbounded exactly where the policy has dropped reference mass, the regime the penalty is meant to police. Here the reference is an explicit categorical over the few legal moves from one network evaluation, so Equation (2) is computed exactly with no extra sampling.

Appendix F Strength evaluation protocol

Searchless Elo is fit with BayesElo from a closed round-robin among the conditions—the frozen base and the fine-tuned agents—all playing searchless: each move is the arg​max\argmax of a single policy forward pass. Openings are sampled from the UHO (Unbalanced Human Openings) book—slightly unbalanced positions that lower the draw rate and sharpen resolution between closely matched engines—and paired, each played from both colors; games are capped at 512512 plies. Every pair of swept models plays 200200 games (100100 paired openings), and each model additionally plays 1,0001{,}000 games (500500 paired openings) against the base. The fit fixes the base at the scale’s zero; we place the ladder on an absolute axis by identifying that zero with the Chessformer paper’s rating of the same network, 2374±372374\pm 37 (Monroe et al., 2026), an external anchor whose ±37\pm 37 uncertainty shifts all ratings together and leaves within-pool differences unchanged. The Δ\DeltaElo intervals in Table 1 (≈±8.3\approx\!\pm 8.3) are the BayesElo 95%95\% intervals from these game counts. They reflect game-sampling variance for one fixed pair of checkpoints per cell; we do not repeat the fine-tuning across seeds, so they do not capture training-run variance, and given the small gains the ranking among the top cells should be read as indicative rather than seed-stable. Because the rating is fit over the whole pool, a model’s ladder position and its direct head-to-head record against the base can diverge—some models that rate near zero outscore the base directly, and vice versa—so Table 1 reports the direct record alongside the ladder. Finally, the 23742374 anchor is the Chessformer paper’s engine round-robin rating for this network, on a different scale from the human online-pool (Lichess) Elo sometimes quoted for searchless networks, so the absolute value is comparable only within engine-versus-engine play.

Appendix G Training configuration

Optimization.

Table 2 lists the settings; this appendix gives the reasoning behind them. We use AdamW (β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.98\beta_{2}=0.98, weight decay 00) with a 200200-step linear warmup from zero to the per-group peak, held constant for the remaining 1,8001{,}800 steps, for 2,0002{,}000 total optimizer steps. We use layerwise learning rates: 3×10−63{\times}10^{-6} on the backbone, 1×10−51{\times}10^{-5} on its final block, 1×10−51{\times}10^{-5} on the policy head, and 3×10−53{\times}10^{-5} on the value head. The final transformer block is treated as part of the policy readout rather than a generic backbone layer, because in Chessformer it is the block that resolves move-specific features for the policy head (Lin et al., 2026); we therefore match its rate to the policy head’s so the layer producing the move logits adapts as fast as the head consuming them. The value head, unconstrained by the forward-KL prior and fit by a low-bias EMA-stabilized bootstrap, takes the largest rate. The value-loss coefficient is cv=0.2c_{v}=0.2, the EMA decay is α=0.995\alpha=0.995, and the importance-sampling cap is exactly 11. We apply no gradient clipping and train in float32 precision; dropout and stochastic depth are off during fine-tuning.

Self-play, data, and sweep.

Each iteration consumes one transition from each of N=1,024N=1{,}024 parallel games, so 2,0002{,}000 steps cover ≈2.05\approx 2.05M transitions. Games are capped at 512512 plies (scored as draws at the cap), with standard chess termination otherwise. The headline forward-KL weight is β=10−2\beta=10^{-2}, chosen exactly as every other arm’s was, on the 10,00010{,}000-puzzle suite (Table 6) and confirmed at scale by Figure 5; each baseline in Table 1 is likewise reported at its own swept-best coefficient. Searchless Elo is the closed arg​max\argmax round-robin of Appendix F (200200 games per swept model pair and 1,0001{,}000 games against the base). Coefficient selection uses the 10,00010{,}000-puzzle suite of Ruoss et al. (2024) (Table 6); the reported accuracies use the uniformly sampled 100,000100{,}000-puzzle and the ≥2400\geq\!2400-rated 20,00020{,}000-puzzle Lichess suites (Table 1) and the mate-in-NN suites of Lin et al. (2026), with mate-in-5 restricted to exact five-move mates (Table 3). Every cell uses the same 2,0002{,}000-step, 1,0241{,}024-game budget, so compute is matched across conditions.

Beyond Search-Imitation:
Prior-Directed Exploration for Searchless Chess
Szymon Miłosz*
Piotr Duch
Szymon Grabowski
Affiliation: Institute of Applied Computer Science, Lodz University of Technology
Affiliation: *Corresponding author:
szymon.milosz@dokt.p.lodz.pl
Abstract
Searchless chess networks reach human master strength from a single forward pass by imitating a
stronger teacher: the strongest, Leela Chess Zero’s (Lc0) released Chessformer, distills the visit
counts of an AlphaZero-style Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). Imitating a search is a poor proxy for
playing without one, so we fine-tune for single-pass strength with self-play reinforcement learning
(RL). Its exploration is usually supplied by an entropy bonus—the reverse Kullback–Leibler (KL)
divergence to uniform. We replace it with a forward, mass-covering KL toward the network’s own
MCTS prior—prior-directed exploration—so exploration covers the moves the prior judges
promising, and pair it with an entropy-adaptive sampling temperature, set by the value head’s
outcome uncertainty, that sharpens once a position is decided. In about two thousand steps it
raises puzzle accuracy from 93.9%93.9\% to 94.9%94.9\% on a 100,000100{,}000-puzzle suite and mate-in-four
accuracy from 77%77\% to 81%81\% while holding searchless strength at or slightly above the base.
Measuring tactical accuracy and playing strength together across a matched-compute sweep,
we find the two dissociate: accuracy gains fall in a
one-point band while ratings straddle the base, and a control fine-tuned on puzzles alone posts the study’s largest tactical gains
while shedding roughly 260260 Elo—a better puzzle-solver is not thereby a stronger player.
Distribution-level measurements show what anchoring buys: without a regularizer self-play collapses
onto a single line of play, and the puzzles newly solved are the near misses whose winning
move the prior kept alive. The forward-KL prior tops the rating ladder, statistically tied with a
reverse-KL anchor that concentrates twice as hard and drops the hardest solutions the mass-covering
prior keeps in support.
Keywords: searchless chess; self-play reinforcement learning; exploration;
Kullback–Leibler regularization; policy gradient; transformer policy networks

1 Introduction

A recent line of work builds chess networks that play at up to human master strength11
1
We use
“master” conservatively and avoid “grandmaster,” which we think outruns the evidence. Strength
here is pool-dependent: Ruoss et al. (2024) rate the same searchless agent at 28952895 against
humans in the Lichess blitz pool but at 22992299 in an engine tournament, and the interpretability
study we build on titles our exact checkpoint “grandmaster-level” (Lin et al., 2026). Labels
of that kind rest on online blitz or engine-pool ratings: the only human-facing evidence in this
line is blitz play on Lichess, and the sole reported game record outside it is a five-game
exhibition against a 21002100-rated player. Online pools run well above the over-the-board scale at
equal strength, and none of these networks has been evaluated at classical time controls, where
such a claim would have to be settled.
Our claims are relative to the base network and do not turn on the absolute label. while almost
eliminating test-time search: the move comes from a single forward pass of a policy
(Monroe et al., 2026), a one-ply value lookup over the legal children
(Ruoss et al., 2024), or a fixed, shallow decoding or beam procedure standing in for a tree
search (Ye et al., 2025; Hamara et al., 2025). Every one
of them is trained by imitation: a network is fit to a stronger but slower teacher and then
frozen. Our starting point is the strongest, the Chessformer architecture
(Monroe et al., 2026) as instantiated and trained by Leela Chess Zero (Lc0)
(The LCZero Authors, 2018); it is obtained by supervised distillation of AlphaZero-style self-play data, fitting
its policy head to the search’s MCTS visit-count distribution and its value head to game
outcomes. We write “Chessformer” for this released network from here on. Imitating a search is
mismatched with playing without one in two ways. The target is mismatched, because the
visit-count distribution is only a noisy proxy for the move that maximizes win probability under
direct, searchless play. The state distribution is mismatched, because the training games
were produced with search while the weaker searchless policy, left to its own devices, reaches a
different distribution of positions, the covariate shift familiar from imitation learning.
Self-play RL removes both at once: it optimizes a win/draw/loss reward for searchless strength on
data drawn from the searchless policy’s own play. We use it to push Chessformer beyond its
search-imitation training.
Interpretability studies of Lc0’s transformer chess networks make the target mismatch concrete:
these networks carry rich internal computation—with evidence even of learned look-ahead to
future optimal moves (Jenner et al., 2024)—yet on tactical puzzles with a single winning move,
that move is often computed in the intermediate layers only for the final layer to override it in
favor of a safer, positional alternative; a targeted intervention against this late-layer safety bias
has been shown to reverse the override for a majority of the suppressed wins (Sandmann et al., 2025)
(observed on a smaller network of the same square-token lineage rather than on our exact checkpoint;
Appendix B).
Because searchless play commits to the arg​max\argmax, such an override costs strength outright, and we
conjecture that fine-tuning on game outcomes restores the move’s rank—reaching through training the
correction their activation steering reaches at inference.
Reinforcement learning improves a policy only to the extent that it explores, and policy-gradient
methods sustain exploration with an entropy bonus that keeps the action distribution spread out
(Williams, 1992; Williams and Peng, 1991; Mnih et al., 2016; Schulman et al., 2017; Haarnoja et al., 2018). The entropy bonus is
indifferent to which moves are worth trying. Up to an additive constant it is the negative
KL divergence −DKL(πθ∥𝒰)-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}\,\big\|\,\mathcal{U}\right) to the uniform distribution 𝒰\mathcal{U}, so it pushes
probability onto all legal moves, including the many that no strong player would consider. With a
large branching factor this spends the exploration budget on obviously bad moves and gives a weak,
undirected signal; the same uninformed spreading, and its converse entropy collapse, are live
concerns in language-model RL (Cui et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025).
A far better reference is already available at no extra cost: the base network’s own policy. The
network was trained to match the MCTS visit-count distributions of a self-play search, so a single
forward pass already returns a search-derived map of the moves worth examining—not the search
itself, but the network’s distilled approximation of it. We use this policy πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} as the
exploration reference, replacing the entropy bonus with a forward, mass-covering KL penalty
DKL(πbase∥πθ)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\theta}\right) toward it. Direction is what turns a divergence
into an exploration signal: the mass-covering KL diverges whenever the policy drops a move the
prior considers promising, forcing the policy to keep covering the prior’s informed support,
whereas the mode-seeking DKL(πθ∥πbase)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\right), the anchoring penalty of reinforcement learning
from human feedback (RLHF) and from verifiable rewards (RLVR)
(Ouyang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024), would let the policy collapse onto one move.
Using the mass-covering direction for exploration has appeared recently in language-model RL
(Deng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025); we adapt it as a drop-in replacement for the entropy
bonus, toward a fixed search-derived prior, in searchless chess. We call the mechanism
prior-directed exploration; Section 4 places it among the alternatives.
Prior-directed exploration helps only when the reference is itself exploratory, spreading mass
over several promising moves rather than one, so that there is breadth worth covering.
Search-derived policies satisfy this by construction, which is why the MCTS prior plays a double
role here: a noisy pointwise target for imitation, but an excellent exploratory
reference for RL. The late-layer demotion described above (Sandmann et al., 2025) illustrates
this split directly: the winning move the output passes over is not erased but re-ranked just below
the top, so it persists in the policy’s distribution with substantial mass—failing as a pointwise
target yet remaining precisely the support a coverage-preserving penalty can keep while the reward
lifts it back (Section 3.5 measures this: the solution sits at rank two in 71%71\%
of the base’s failures). During fine-tuning the win/draw/loss reward re-sharpens the policy within the
prior’s support toward what actually wins, while the forward KL keeps it from collapsing
(Figure 1 previews the outcome on exact mates).
Contributions.
•
We cast strengthening a searchless network as moving beyond search-imitation and
instantiate it as self-play RL that optimizes Chessformer’s single-pass strength directly,
addressing the noisy-target and distribution-shift mismatches of imitation, in a single-step
self-play recipe: truncated importance sampling and a one-step temporal-difference (TD(0)) value
head with an exponential-moving-average (EMA) target
(Sections 2.3–3).
•
For exploration we replace the entropy bonus with a forward, mass-covering KL toward the
network’s own MCTS visit-count prior, prior-directed exploration, adapting a mechanism
recently used in language-model RL (Deng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025) to a fixed external
prior whose support is worth covering; we further argue (Appendix C) that a
search-distilled prior is exploratory by construction (Section 2.2).
•
We introduce an entropy-adaptive sampling temperature that sets each move’s
temperature to the value head’s win/draw/loss uncertainty, so self-play terminates once a
position is decided yet stays exploratory while it is live (Section 2.3).
•
Empirically, where the interpretability studies of these networks probe them almost entirely
through tactical puzzles, we show prior-directed fine-tuning improves both tactics and
searchless strength—modestly on strength, in about two thousand steps.
We further quantify, under matched compute, that tactical accuracy and playing strength
dissociate, so the coupling rests on anchoring exploration to the prior rather than on
tactical optimization alone; and we show the tactical gains are retention-gated:
fine-tuning promotes near misses the base still ranked second or third and recovers nothing whose
solution the base had driven below πbase≈0.05\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\!\approx\!0.05 (Section 3).
•
We define and measure two coverage-versus-collapse diagnostics—trajectory coverage
ΩKN\Omega^{N}_{K} and the solution probability of sampling a ground-truth winning line in one
pass. Both split as the mechanism predicts: the unregularized policy collapses onto a single
opening line, and the mode-seeking anchor concentrates about twice as hard as the forward prior
and drops the hardest solutions, where the forward prior retains them
(Section 3).

2.1 Background: policy gradients and entropy regularization
We work with policy-gradient RL: a stochastic policy πθ​(a∣s)\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s) is improved by ascending the

the best move has been found. The failure is self-sealing: a policy-gradient update credits only the
moves it actually samples, so once a move’s probability reaches zero its reward is never observed
again and no gradient can restore it—exploration must keep candidate moves sampled for their

Why the forward direction.
Direction is the crux, and Figure 2 lays out the asymmetry in full. Our penalty
DKL(πbase∥πθ)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\theta}\right) takes the forward, mass-covering direction—in the usual terminology
zero-avoiding—so minimizing it forces the policy to keep
probability on every move the
prior deems promising, which is exactly what an exploration signal should do—it prevents collapse
to a near-deterministic strategy, and the moves it must cover are the prior’s high-probability ones
rather than the whole action set. The reverse KL DKL(πθ∥πbase)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\right) is mode-seeking and
zero-forcing (Minka, 2005) instead—the anchoring penalty of KL-regularized policy optimization, from
behavior priors to RLHF and RLVR
(Galashov et al., 2019; Ouyang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024; Tirumala et al., 2022).
That is the right property for the
anchor’s job, which is to confine the policy to a trusted reference’s support—in RLHF so that a
learned reward cannot be over-optimized by drifting off it (reward hacking)—but as an
exploration driver it would
license the very collapse we are trying to prevent: the two uses want opposite failure modes from
the same divergence. We are deliberate about the word
“exploration”: the forward KL sustains coverage of the prior’s promising moves and prevents
collapse onto one of them, but being zero where πbase​(a)→0\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(a)\to 0 it cannot drive discovery of strong
moves outside the prior’s support. It preserves prior-anchored breadth rather than seeking
novelty, unlike the intrinsic-motivation methods of Section 4.
Relation to entropy regularization, and the requirement on the prior.
Entropy regularization is the reverse KL to the uniform reference
(Equation (1)), and even there the directions are not interchangeable: the
forward KL to uniform DKL(𝒰∥πθ)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\mathcal{U}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\theta}\right) is the label-smoothing penalty
(Pereyra et al., 2017), not the entropy bonus. Both share a minimizer against a uniform
reference, so either one merely spreads mass over all moves; prior-directed exploration keeps the
mass-covering direction and swaps that uninformative reference for the prior, turning uniform
spreading into coverage of the prior’s promising moves. Because the penalty forces πθ\pi_{\theta} to
cover the support of πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}}, it is only as useful as that support: a near-deterministic expert
would pull the policy onto one move and reproduce collapse, so the method pairs naturally with
priors that are themselves products of exploration, such as MCTS visit-count policies.
Our prior meets that condition by construction, in two steps. First, the targets the search exports
are high-entropy exactly where exploration matters: the predictor-guided upper-confidence rule
(PUCT) keeps visiting every move with appreciable prior until its count catches up, so the exported distribution
πmcts​(a∣s)∝N​(s,a)1/τ\pi_{\mathrm{mcts}}(a\mid s)\propto N(s,a)^{1/\tau} retains mass on several moves wherever more
than one is reasonable and sharpens only where the search itself is confident. Second, the released
network was fit to those targets by cross-entropy, which is the forward KL
DKL(πmcts∥πbase)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\mathrm{mcts}}\,\big\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{base}}\right) up to the target’s own entropy—the same mass-covering
direction we use here—so a network that collapsed onto one move would pay a large loss at every
position where the search spread its visits, and the breadth transfers to the single-pass policy.
The prior we cover is therefore the product of a search, not a runtime search itself, and the
argument does not turn on the particular search variant; Appendix C gives it in full.
How much coverage results under the full objective also depends on β\beta and the reward scale
(GX-Chen et al., 2025), which we set empirically.
A second enabling condition is computational: the forward KL needs the reference’s full
distribution at each state, which is immediate for an enumerable categorical over the legal moves
but expensive for a language model over its vocabulary, one reason the reverse direction is the
default in large-scale post-training (Appendix E).

outcome uncertainty, not move criticality, so μ\mu also sharpens in the relatively rare position whose outcome

dependable given the base’s conversion strength but not infallible. Sampling from
μ\mu rather than πθ\pi_{\theta} makes the batch off-policy, which we correct with a truncated importance
weight in the style of V-trace (Espeholt et al., 2018); τ\tau is computed from the EMA value
head for stability (Appendix E).

3 Experiments
We ask whether prior-directed exploration improves a searchless engine over its base—in
tactical accuracy and in playing strength, without the regression that tactical optimization alone
can cause—holding the rest of the pipeline fixed. The experiments test four things: whether
self-play RL moves the supervised base beyond search-imitation in tactics and in strength; whether
tactical accuracy and playing strength move together or dissociate across exploration terms; how the
forward-KL prior compares with the entropy bonus, a reverse-KL anchor, and no regularizer at equal
compute; and how much each component of the recipe contributes.
3.1 Setup and metrics
Setup and conditions.
Starting from the same frozen Chessformer reference, the publicly released Lc0 checkpoint
BT4-1024x15x32h-swa-6147500 (architecture in Appendix B), we fine-tune with the procedure of
Section 2.3, varying only the exploration term and holding the
network, optimizer, self-play budget, and evaluation fixed. All play and evaluation are searchless.
Four fine-tuned conditions share that pipeline—(i) no regularizer; (ii) the
entropy bonus; (iii) a reverse-KL anchor to πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}}; and (iv) the forward-KL
prior (ours)—and all are measured against the frozen base, the reference to beat. The four
are matched on regularization strength and compute. Each
arm’s coefficient β⋆\beta^{\star} is selected by overall accuracy on the 10,00010{,}000-puzzle suite described
under Metrics below—10−210^{-2} for five of the six term–temperature arms, 10−410^{-4} for the sixth (the entropy
bonus without the adaptive temperature)—and every subsequent evaluation uses the selected model
(Table 6, Appendix G). Ratings carry 95%95\% confidence intervals (one run per cell;
Appendix F); the full training configuration is in Table 2 and Appendix G.
Ablation design.
The runs cross two factors: the exploration term with its coefficient β\beta, and the
entropy-adaptive sampling temperature against a fixed τ≡1\tau\equiv 1 baseline, so that the
temperature’s contribution is separated from the exploration term’s. For each
regularizer we sweep β\beta over the same five-point decade grid from 10−410^{-4} to 11, so that
every arm is selected on identical footing (Appendix G lists the full matrix). Fixing the term and varying β\beta locates each
method’s best operating point on that suite (Table 6); fixing β\beta and
varying the temperature isolates the adaptive temperature; the no-regularizer runs anchor both axes.
Metrics.
Playing strength is reported two ways in Table 1: relative searchless Elo from a closed
round-robin, which resolves within-pool differences and reaches an absolute axis only through a
single external anchor on the base, and each model’s direct record over 1,0001{,}000 games against the
base—its win–draw–loss (W–D–L) record, and the BayesElo likelihood of superiority (LOS) that it
is the stronger player. The protocol is in Appendix F.
Tactical accuracy is measured on three suites of Lichess puzzles. The first is the
10,00010{,}000-puzzle suite released by Ruoss et al. (2024) and reported again in the
Chessformer evaluation (Monroe et al., 2026); scoring on it keeps our base comparable with
the published figure for the same network (Appendix B), and we use it to select
each arm’s coefficient (Table 6). Ten thousand puzzles are too few for the
comparisons this paper turns on, however: the 95%95\% Wilson interval at that size is
≈±0.45\approx\!\pm 0.45 percentage points, while the fine-tuned arms separate by a few tenths of a
point. We therefore built two larger suites, sampling the public Lichess puzzle database the same
way: a uniformly sampled 100,000100{,}000-puzzle suite, which tightens the interval to
≈±0.15\approx\!\pm 0.15 points, and a 20,00020{,}000-puzzle suite restricted to puzzles rated
≥2400\geq\!2400, which spends the sample where the base still fails and the arms still differ. Those ratings are Lichess’s Glicko-2 estimates from human solve rates, so they order puzzles by human difficulty rather than by engine depth—a signal regular enough that predicting it from the board is itself a studied task (Miłosz and Kapusta, 2024; Miłosz, 2025). These
two carry every headline accuracy in the paper (Table 1).
Exploration versus collapse plays out over sequences, so to tie strength to mechanism we add two
sequence-level diagnostics, trajectory coverage and the solution probability,
defined next.
Trajectory coverage ΩKN\Omega^{N}_{K}.
From a state ss we draw complete depth-NN trajectories from the policy’s play
distribution without replacement: a draw samples a continuation move by move, its trajectory
probability πθ​(ξ∣s)=∏t=1Nπθ​(at∣st−1)\pi_{\theta}(\xi\mid s)=\prod_{t=1}^{N}\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t-1}) is recorded, and that mass is
removed from the tree and the remainder renormalized (implemented by subtracting the trajectory’s
mass along its path), so the next draw samples among the lines not yet seen. The coverage after KK
draws,
ΩKN​(s)=𝔼⁡[∑i=1Kπθ​(ξi∣s)],\Omega^{N}_{K}(s)=\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{i=1}^{K}\pi_{\theta}(\xi_{i}\mid s)\Big],
(8)
with the expectation over the sampling and each πθ​(ξi∣s)\pi_{\theta}(\xi_{i}\mid s) evaluated under the original
policy, is the total mass of the KK distinct lines drawn: a near-deterministic policy reaches
ΩKN≈1\Omega^{N}_{K}\approx 1 within a handful of draws, while a policy that spreads mass over many promising
continuations needs thousands. Sweeping KK at fixed NN traces a coverage curve whose shape
distinguishes collapse from prior-directed spreading, the multi-step counterpart of the single-state
coverage and entropy diagnostics; sampled models are drawn through the same play distribution used in
self-play (the tempered μ\mu for adaptive-temperature models), so the curve measures how quickly
self-play exhausts what the policy will actually play.
Solution probability, via the solution negative log-likelihood (NLL).
Tactics accuracy scores whether the arg​max\argmax move solves a puzzle, which is harsh on a stochastic policy
that ranks the solution highly without making it the single most probable move. Each puzzle specifies a
ground-truth line ξ⋆=(a1⋆,…,aM⋆)\xi^{\star}=(a^{\star}_{1},\dots,a^{\star}_{M}) visiting positions
s0⋆,…,sM−1⋆s^{\star}_{0},\dots,s^{\star}_{M-1}, with a set W⁡(st⋆)W(s^{\star}_{t}) of winning moves at each position (usually
the single at+1⋆a^{\star}_{t+1}; where several moves win, all are credited). Per puzzle we compute the
solution NLL, the log-mass the policy keeps along the line,
ℓ(ξ⋆)=−∑t=1Mlog∑a∈W⁡(st−1⋆)πθ(a∣st−1⋆),\ell(\xi^{\star})=-\sum_{t=1}^{M}\log\!\!\sum_{a\in W(s^{\star}_{t-1})}\!\!\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s^{\star}_{t-1}),
(9)
in nats, and report the solution probability p⋆=e−ℓ⁡(ξ⋆)p^{\star}=e^{-\ell(\xi^{\star})}—the
probability of sampling the entire line ξ⋆\xi^{\star} in one rollout (exactly
∏tπθ​(at⋆∣st−1⋆)\prod_{t}\pi_{\theta}(a^{\star}_{t}\mid s^{\star}_{t-1}) when each position admits a single winning move).
Aggregation happens in the log domain: averaging ℓ\ell over puzzles and exponentiating yields the
geometric-mean solution probability, which we report unless stated otherwise. The geometric
mean is the right default for retention because the probability is a product along the line and
heavy losses should not be masked: a policy that drives one solution toward zero probability is
charged in full, where the arithmetic mean can stay high on the strength of the
solutions it keeps (e.g., solution probabilities 0.90.9, 0.8990.899, and 0.0010.001 across three puzzles give an arithmetic mean of 0.6000.600 but a geometric mean of only 0.0930.093)—a divergence between the two means is itself a collapse signal, which
Section 3.3 exploits. Paired model comparisons are likewise made in the log
domain (per-puzzle NLL differences, reported as probability ratios). We compute ℓ\ell under the
untempered πθ\pi_{\theta} (EMA weights), so it measures the learned policy’s intrinsic retention of the
solution rather than the tempered behavior policy’s, and it rewards exactly the property
prior-directed exploration is meant to preserve: keeping the correct line in support.

3.2 Searchless playing strength
Because the gains are small, we read the ladder and the direct record together. Self-play moves
the base, but modestly. The forward-KL prior at fixed temperature tops the ladder at +16.6±8.3+16.6\pm 8.3
Elo over the 23742374 base; head-to-head it outscores the base 0.520.52 over 1,0001{,}000 games
(361361–318318–321321 W–D–L, likelihood of superiority 0.940.94)—a real but slender edge, short of
decisive. The reverse-KL anchor is tied on the ladder (+16.2±8.3+16.2\pm 8.3) and in fact wins its own match
against the base more clearly (0.550.55, LOS >0.99>0.99), so on strength the two prior-anchored directions
are indistinguishable and we do not claim the forward direction is the stronger player. We read
the ladder cautiously for a second reason: a closed-pool rating and a direct record can
diverge—the unregularized fixed-temperature run rates near zero on the ladder yet outscores the base
0.530.53 head-to-head—because the rating reflects play against the whole pool, not the base alone.
Two
further cautions apply. The headline is the largest of many swept configurations, so part of its
margin is selection (winner’s-curse) inflation the per-row interval does not capture. And the
exploration term’s own contribution is modest and temperature-dependent: at fixed temperature the
forward-KL prior adds ≈17\approx\!17 Elo over no regularizer (+16.6+16.6 versus −0.5-0.5), but with the
adaptive temperature, which alone already reaches +9.8+9.8, it adds only ≈2\approx\!2 (+11.7+11.7 versus
+9.8+9.8)—prior and temperature are partly substitutes. What the strength results do establish is the
coarse ordering—anchoring exploration to the prior helps and clearly beats the fragile entropy
bonus, whose rating is acutely sensitive to its coefficient: without the adaptive temperature it
peaks at just +6.6+6.6 Elo (its selected β=10−4\beta=10^{-4}) and falls to −119-119 by β=10−2\beta=10^{-2} and
−576-576 at β=1\beta=1 (Table 6 tracks the accompanying accuracy collapse)—while the forward-versus-reverse
question turns on move-distribution behavior the Elo cannot see, which
Sections 3.3 and 3.4 take up.

3.3 Tactical accuracy, retention, and coverage
With the arms fixed by that selection, we turn from strength to the policies themselves: how
tactical accuracy responds to the coefficient, how much probability each policy retains on winning
lines, and how concentrated its play becomes.
Coefficient sweep.
To trace the shape of the response rather than merely locate its optimum, we re-evaluate the
headline forward-KL-with-adaptive-temperature arm on the 100,000100{,}000-puzzle suite and add four
intermediate half-decade points, giving the nine-point curve of Figure 5; these
extra points are for resolution only and play no part in selection. The larger suite’s 95%95\%
intervals of about ±0.14\pm 0.14 percentage points resolve differences the 10,00010{,}000-puzzle suite
could not. The
response to β\beta has a clean single minimum. The frozen base errs on 6.15%6.15\% of the puzzles and
the unregularized run (β=0\beta=0) on 5.94%5.94\%, so self-play already helps; adding the forward-KL
prior helps further, with the error falling to 5.13%5.13\% at β=10−2\beta=10^{-2}, 1.021.02 percentage

The response is U-shaped in log⁡β\log\beta with its trough near
β∈[3⋅10−3,3⋅10−2]\beta\in[3\cdot 10^{-3},3\cdot 10^{-2}], set between two limits the sweep approaches without

beats the entropy bonus—a U-shaped response to a coefficient is generic to regularizers.

mate-in-5). The two directions split exactly as the mechanism predicts. The mode-seeking reverse
anchor is sharper where lines are short, its retained probability 11–4%4\% higher (as a ratio) on
the full tactics suite and on mates in one to three, while the mass-covering forward prior wins
increasingly with difficulty and depth: its solution probability is 33%33\% higher on the
≥2400\geq\!2400 puzzles (paired ratio 1.331.33) and 11%11\% and 34%34\%
higher at mate-in-4 and 5. The ≥2400\geq\!2400 subset
shows the collapse signature directly, in the two means of Table 4: the reverse
anchor’s arithmetic-mean solution probability (0.570.57) tops the forward prior’s (0.530.53) and
nearly doubles the base’s (0.300.30), yet its geometric mean falls below even the base’s—it seizes
some hard solutions outright while dropping others toward zero probability, where the forward prior
keeps nearly all of them in support. The unregularized run is the same failure at its limit: the
highest arithmetic mean in the study (0.600.60) against a geometric mean of 0.010.01, a sixty-fold
gap. Binned by puzzle rating on the 100,000100{,}000-puzzle suite (Figure 6,

anchor’s retention collapses well below the base’s (−0.38-0.38 nats) while the forward prior’s stays
near it.
Argmax accuracy follows the same gradient, with a turn at the top: both prior-anchored models gain
under a tenth of a point where the base already saturates below rating 1,0001{,}000, rising to
+3.5+3.5 points in the 2,4002{,}400–2,6002{,}600 bin before falling back to +1.8+1.8 on the hardest puzzles,
where nearly half the base’s failures stay out of reach.
The entropy bonus makes the third corner of the comparison, and it fails in the opposite way. Its
adaptive-temperature model—the strongest arg​max\argmax puzzle-solver among the self-play runs
(Table 1)—retains dramatically less of every solution than the base does:
0.2220.222 versus 0.6600.660 on the tactics suite, 0.1030.103 versus 0.1990.199 on its ≥2400\geq\!2400 puzzles, and
0.3990.399 versus 0.9150.915 even at mate-in-1, where its arg​max\argmax accuracy is at ceiling (losses of
0.830.83–2.712.71 nats across the mate depths and 0.530.53–1.341.34 nats across the rating bins). This is
not the reverse anchor’s mode-seeking collapse but the uninformed spreading of
Section 2.1 made visible: the entropy bonus leaves the top move in place while
flattening the distribution around it, so the arg​max\argmax stays right as the mass a training run would
need to sample drains away. The three regularizers thus separate cleanly at the distribution level
even where arg​max\argmax metrics tie.
Trajectory coverage.
Retention asks about ground-truth lines; the trajectory coverage ΩKN\Omega^{N}_{K} asks how concentrated
the policy’s own play is (Section 3.1). We draw depth-44 trajectories from the

(Figure 7). Covering 95%95\% of the mass—out of 197,281197{,}281 legal

unregularized run needs exactly one in both variants, a single

(Figure 10).

3.4 Policy shape: concentration, coverage, and sampled play
The trajectory-coverage diagnostic of Section 3.3 measures how concentrated each
policy’s play is; here we tie that concentration to strength and add three single-state
diagnostics of the policies themselves. We run a second closed round-robin over the
ten configurations of Figure 10 in Appendix H—the frozen base sampled raw and through the
tempered μ\mu, and each exploration term at both temperatures—in which every model samples
its move rather than taking the arg​max\argmax, playing through the behavior policy it used in self-play
(Equation (6); a τ≡1\tau\!\equiv\!1 arm plays its raw πθ\pi_{\theta}). Alongside the
resulting ratings, Table 5 reports three diagnostics of the policy each model
actually plays: its move-distribution entropy, its two KL divergences to the raw base, and how much
of its mass stays on the base’s top moves.
Under sampling, strength becomes a read-out of concentration. The ratings span ≈670\approx\!670 Elo,
more than twenty times the arg​max\argmax ladder’s ≈30\approx\!30 (Table 1), and they track
move entropy inversely: the more a policy concentrates, the better it plays when its moves
are sampled, because a diffuse policy squanders draws on its low-probability tail. This is a
diagnostic of the policies’ shape, not a second measure of playing skill—the arg​max\argmax ladder is the
strength result, and the sampled ordering (in which the reverse arm edges the forward by a margin
the arg​max\argmax ladder does not show, tracking its slightly harder concentration in
Figure 10) merely re-scores how sharp each policy is. The adaptive temperature
is visible directly: tempering the base lifts it +361+361 Elo by sharpening its play (H\Ent from
1.691.69 to 0.390.39), and every adaptive arm outranks its τ≡1\tau\!\equiv\!1 twin.

3.5 What fine-tuning recovers
The two prior-anchored models newly solve 1,4051{,}405 and 1,3781{,}378 puzzles the base
fails (and give back 383383 and 398398, for the net gains of Table 1), and the
retention machinery above predicts which: improvement must be sampled before it can be
reinforced (Section 2.1), so the failures fine-tuning can fix should be
exactly those whose solution the base still plays with non-negligible probability. That is what we
find (Figure 8). The policy is Markovian, so we score recovery at the level of
positions, under the multi-solution ground truth of Table 1 (a move is correct if
it is an optimal mate or the marked move): on the 100,000100{,}000-puzzle suite the base plays a wrong
move at 6,8406{,}840 of its 231,739231{,}739 solver positions, and a position counts as recovered when the
fine-tuned model’s move there is correct—the forward prior recovers 1,5951{,}595 of them, the
reverse anchor 1,5601{,}560. Binned by the probability the base retains on the solution at the
position, recovery is gated: neither model recovers any of the 390390 positions with
πbase​(solution)<0.05\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\text{solution})<0.05, they recover about 4%4\% of the 1,3451{,}345 in
[0.05,0.15)[0.05,0.15), 2121–22%22\% of the 2,8972{,}897 in [0.15,0.3)[0.15,0.3), and about 41%41\% of the 2,2082{,}208
above 0.30.3 (geometric-mean retention of 0.300.30/0.310.31 at recovered positions versus 0.170.17 at
unrecovered). The rank view says the same thing more sharply: at 71%71\% of the base’s wrong
positions the solution is ranked second, and these recover at 29%29\%, falling to 11%11\% at
rank 33 and about 5%5\% at ranks 44–55; none of the 186186 positions with the solution at rank
66 or deeper is recovered by either model, and the deepest recovered solution sat at rank 55.
The gap that had to be closed is correspondingly narrow: at recovered positions the base’s top
move led the solution by a median of 6.56.5 percentage points, against 2424 points at the
positions that stay wrong. Fine-tuning, under either
anchor, is near-miss promotion: it reorders the top of the distribution the prior kept
alive, and it never resurrects a move the base had effectively discarded.
Recovery, where it happens, is decisive: the fine-tuned policies place a mean 3636/4242
additional percentage points of mass on the recovered solutions (medians 3535/4343), and the
puzzles gained are hard ones—mean rating 2,0282{,}028/2,0202{,}020, far above the base’s solved set
(1,4291{,}429) though below its average failure (2,1902{,}190), as the retention gate predicts. The
give-backs are the same trade in reverse, still near misses (on 93%93\%/92%92\% the solution
remains at rank 22 of the fine-tuned output) and shallow—the probability leaked off those
solutions has median 5.85.8/7.77.7 points, against the 3636/4242-point surges of the recoveries.
Give-back is gated from above as recovery is gated from below: of the more than 200,000200{,}000
positions where the base’s top move leads the runner-up by over 0.60.6, neither model gives back a
single one. Losing a puzzle is an arg​max\argmax flip between two close moves; gaining one is a
commitment. The value
head moves with the policy: at recovered positions the base’s win-minus-loss estimate has median
0.020.02—the value head barely sees the win it is failing to play—and fine-tuning lifts it to
0.080.08/0.100.10, while at unrecovered positions, where the base already reads the position more
clearly (0.180.18), it changes little (0.170.17/0.190.19).
Where the two anchors differ.
The two anchors recover a large shared core and a small distinct fringe—1,1981{,}198 puzzles both
fix, plus 207207 exclusive to the forward prior and 180180 to the reverse anchor—and the fringes
differ in kind. The forward prior’s exclusive recoveries reach lower into the retained tail and
are the harder puzzles: median base solution probability 0.2850.285 and mean rating 2,1392{,}139,
against the reverse anchor’s 0.2970.297 and 2,0992{,}099. This is the per-puzzle face of the retention
split of Table 4: the mass-covering prior holds probability on hard, deep solutions
that the mode-seeking anchor lets go, and those are the wins only it can then promote.
Appendix H walks through three exclusive recoveries of each anchor
(Figure 9), annotating every candidate move with the base’s own value-head
verdict and a Stockfish oracle; in five of the six positions the base’s value head already
separates the winning move from the played one, so the first time self-play samples the retained
move, the advantage signal is immediate.
3.6 Tactical accuracy versus playing strength
That any single evaluation figure is an imperfect proxy for playing strength is itself
known—a searchless transformer’s rating swings some 600600 points between the human and engine
pools it is measured in (Ruoss et al., 2024), and the imitation-versus-strength split is the
premise of McIlroy-Young et al. (2020)—but our matched-compute sweep lets us quantify how wide
the tactics-versus-strength gap is here, and it is wide. Across the
eight fine-tuned configurations of Table 1 the two axes move independently: every one
that improves overall accuracy does so within a narrow band (+0.15+0.15 to +1.05+1.05 percentage points)
while ratings range from −5.8-5.8 to +16.6+16.6 Elo and straddle the base. The clearest case
among the self-play runs is the entropy bonus with adaptive temperature, which posts the
highest overall puzzle accuracy of any of them (94.90%94.90\%, +1.05+1.05 percentage points) yet earns no
playing strength: its rating
(−5.8-5.8 Elo) is statistically indistinguishable from the base, its interval spanning zero and its
head-to-head score 0.490.49. Pushed harder the split turns to caricature: an entropy coefficient of 11
still answers 83.1%83.1\% of the 10,00010{,}000-puzzle suite correctly (Table 6) while
losing 933933 of its 1,0001{,}000 games to the base.
Starker still is a control that optimizes puzzles directly: fine-tuning the same base for the
same 2,0002{,}000 steps by supervised learning on the puzzle solutions rather than by self-play RL
(Table 1, last row). Its training pool is drawn from the Lichess puzzle database with
both evaluation suites removed, so it is scored on positions it has never seen. It
posts by far the largest tactical gains in the study—overall accuracy
→96.80%93.85\!\to\!96.80\%
(+2.95+2.95 percentage points) and on the ≥2400\geq\!2400 suite →67.95%60.01\!\to\!67.95\% (+7.94+7.94 percentage points), around three times the
largest gain from any RL condition—yet its searchless rating collapses to −258.0±9.1-258.0\pm 9.1 Elo,
roughly a one-in-five score against the base. The cause is the state-distribution mismatch of
Section 1, here induced on purpose: supervising on a fixed external set of positions
rather than on states from the policy’s own play sharpens move-by-move tactics while whole-game
strength falls apart. The lesson is not that puzzle accuracy is a bad measure—it is the direct
measure of the tactical skill we target, and the dense, cheap signal our coefficient sweeps rely
on—but that it measures a different capability than playing strength: most fine-tuning
recipes lift tactics, while strength is what separates a prior-anchored run that gains a little from
an entropy run that does not gain at all and a puzzle-tuned control that collapses. An evaluation
must therefore carry both axes separately. The forward- and reverse-KL priors are the configurations
that hold both up at once, raising tactical accuracy while keeping strength at or above the base,
and that coupling—not the puzzle figure on its own—is the result that bears on searchless play.
4 Related Work
Searchless chess.
Classical neural engines couple a network with a large test-time search; a recent line almost
removes it, its strongest members playing at human master level. Ruoss et al. (2024) distill Stockfish
action-values into a transformer used as a depth-one move selector, one forward pass per legal
child with no recursion; DiffuSearch folds an implicit search into a discrete-diffusion policy
(Ye et al., 2025); Hamara et al. (2025) navigate a contrastively learned value
embedding; and the Chessformer architecture (Monroe et al., 2026) as trained by Lc0
(The LCZero Authors, 2018), our base and, in engine-versus-engine play, the strongest of these, selects each move from a single forward pass of
its policy head. A related thread interprets how such networks compute without explicit search
(Jenner et al., 2024; Sandmann et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026), and a separate imitation line fits human move
distributions for human-like play rather than maximal strength (McIlroy-Young et al., 2020); a further human-centric line predicts how hard a position is for people, regressing Lichess’s Glicko-2 puzzle ratings from the board (Miłosz and Kapusta, 2024; Miłosz, 2025). The playing systems in this line are
obtained by imitation and then frozen.
RL for games and pretrained policies.
AlphaZero learns strong policies by self-play guided by MCTS (Silver et al., 2018), extended by
MuZero to planning with a learned model (Schrittwieser et al., 2020), and Lc0 trains openly
available networks of this kind (The LCZero Authors, 2018; Monroe et al., 2026). That self-play loop
produces the search-trained network we start from; it does not optimize the network’s own
searchless play. Separately, RL adapts strong pretrained policies, as in RLHF and RLVR, which
fine-tune language models against a reward with a KL anchor to the base
(Ouyang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024). We join the two: we take an externally strong
searchless network and fine-tune it by self-play RL whose objective is searchless strength itself,
neither proposing a new way to obtain the network nor merely anchoring it to its initialization.
Exploration regularizers, and the three roles of the KL.
An entropy bonus is the standard way to maintain exploration and avoid deterministic collapse
(Williams and Peng, 1991; Mnih et al., 2016; Schulman et al., 2017), promoted to part of the objective in
maximum-entropy RL (Haarnoja et al., 2018). Intrinsic-reward methods drive exploration with novelty
signals, count-based bonuses (Bellemare et al., 2016), prediction-error curiosity
(Pathak et al., 2017), and random network distillation (Burda et al., 2019), which modify the
reward rather than the action-distribution regularizer and are orthogonal to what we study. A closer
neighbor is GFlowNets’ mass-covering objective of sampling in proportion to reward
(Bengio et al., 2021), which pursues the same anti-collapse, multi-modal coverage we seek but
enforces it by flow-matching rather than a divergence penalty. Entropy collapse is now a central
concern in language-model post-training (Cui et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025).
GX-Chen et al. (2025) qualify the direction argument we rely on: under KL-regularized RL the
direction fixes only the family of optimal distributions, with mode coverage governed mainly
by the regularization strength and the scale of rewards relative to reference probabilities—which
is why we select β\beta empirically and rest the forward-versus-reverse case on the measured
coverage of Section 3.3 rather than on direction alone. The KL itself
plays three distinct roles in policy optimization: it constrains each update to the previous
policy as a trust region (Kakade, 2002; Schulman et al., 2015; Schulman et al., 2017); it regularizes
toward a fixed reference or learned default, generalizing maximum-entropy RL
(Galashov et al., 2019; Tirumala et al., 2022), underpinning control-as-inference
(Levine, 2018) and maximum a posteriori policy optimisation (MPO)
(Abdolmaleki et al., 2018), and anchoring fine-tuned
models in RLHF and RLVR (Ouyang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024); and, in our use, it drives
exploration. Closest to our setting, Ota et al. (2026) combine the first two roles for
two-player zero-sum games—a reverse KL to the current iterate together with an entropy
bonus—prove local convergence, and evaluate on five board games including a reduced chess; their
agents learn from scratch by self-play, where we adapt an externally strong released network, and
their entropy term points at the uniform distribution where ours points at that network. The
fixed-reference role is conventionally taken in the policy-first, mode-seeking direction
DKL(πθ∥π0)D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}\,\big\|\,\pi_{0}\right), to keep the policy near its reference; the trust-region role is taken in
either direction, reference-first in trust region policy optimization (TRPO) and PPO’s
KL-penalty variant and policy-first in
Ota et al. (2026). The exploration regularizers
above all point at the uniform distribution. We keep the reference-policy regularizer, reverse its
direction, and swap its reference for a fixed, externally strong, search-derived prior.
Forward-KL regularization, and the closest work.
Forward, mass-covering KL toward a reference is well established, but toward ends other than
exploration. Label smoothing adds a forward KL to the uniform distribution
(Szegedy et al., 2016; Pereyra et al., 2017); toward a strong reference, ff-DPO generalizes
direct preference optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023) to ff-divergences including the
forward KL (Wang et al., 2024), and knowledge distillation matches a teacher under the forward KL
(Hinton et al., 2015), which on-policy distillation generalizes to a family of divergences
scored on student-generated data (Agarwal et al., 2024). In all of these the divergence
serves regularization, alignment, or distillation, not exploration. Closest to us, two recent
language-model works turn the forward direction toward exploration: diversity-preserving hybrid RL
(DPH-RL) anchors mass-covering
ff-divergences to the model’s own initial policy as a rehearsal term against diversity
collapse (Li et al., 2025), and rewards-aware policy optimization (RAPO) replaces the reverse-KL anchor with a forward KL to
explore beyond the base model’s support, adding a reward-aware reweighting of the reference
to steer exploration within it (Deng et al., 2025). We differ on three points. We replace the entropy bonus, casting
prior-directed exploration as a generalization of entropy regularization rather than a variant of
the trust-region anchor. Our reference is a fixed, externally strong, search-derived prior used
as is to cover its already-informed support, not the model’s own initial policy or a
reference reweighted to redirect exploration. And our domain is searchless chess, where the target is
playing strength rather than reasoning accuracy.
5 Conclusion
Searchless chess networks are trained to imitate a search and then deployed without one. We argued
that self-play RL is the natural way to close this gap, optimizing single-pass strength directly,
and that the exploration it needs is better served by the network’s own search-derived prior than by
an entropy bonus: replacing the bonus with a forward, mass-covering KL toward the MCTS visit-count
prior drives the policy to cover exactly the moves the prior judges promising, avoiding both
uninformed spreading and mode collapse, while the reward sharpens within that support. In about two
thousand steps, far below the search that produced the network, this delivers a clear tactical
improvement—higher puzzle accuracy and deeper forced mates—while searchless playing strength
holds at or just above the base, the forward-KL prior topping the rating ladder with the reverse-KL
anchor statistically tied.
The finding we underline constrains how such fine-tuning should be read: tactical accuracy and
playing strength dissociate, so a method that lifts puzzle accuracy is not thereby a stronger
player, and the worth of anchoring exploration to the prior is that it improves tactics without
spending strength. The distribution-level measurements separate the two anchoring directions as the
mechanism predicts—the mode-seeking anchor concentrates about twice as hard and drops the hardest
solutions, where the mass-covering prior keeps them, and without any regularizer self-play collapses
onto a single line of play—while the per-puzzle recovery analysis says what fine-tuning can and
cannot fix: it promotes the near misses the prior kept alive and never resurrects a move the base
had discarded, which is why keeping candidates sampled is the exploration term’s whole job.
Chess is a
clean testbed because its search-derived priors are unusually strong. The recipe should extend to
settings that share its two enabling conditions, an enumerable per-state reference and an
exploratory prior worth covering, most naturally other games and combinatorial planning with a
search- or ensemble-derived prior. The standard language-model setting is not excluded in
principle but meets the enumerability condition only at a cost: the forward KL needs the reference’s
full next-token distribution, the O⁡(|V|)O(|V|) teacher pass that on-policy distillation already pays
(Agarwal et al., 2024) but that is dear to add on top of RL exploration (Section 2.2)—so
chess serves here to exhibit the mechanism where the prior is cheap and strong, not to rule language out.
Limitations.
Our claims are scoped to one domain and one base network. The forward-versus-reverse evidence supports
the mechanism on both retention and coverage, but the two directions remain tied on strength,
and the strength gains are small in absolute terms—a reminder that two thousand steps of
fine-tuning adjust the base network rather than remake it.
The method carries two structural requirements. The forward KL is computed exactly only for a categorical distribution over a modest action set; large action spaces require estimation, the cost
that makes the reverse direction the default there. And it helps only when the prior’s support is
worth covering: a weak or biased prior would be faithfully covered, so annealing β\beta or combining
references is a natural extension. Neither
evaluation axis is a reliable arbiter alone either—self-play Elo can flatter a pool with shared blind
spots, and tactical accuracy can rise even for a weaker player—so we claim improvements only where both
agree.
Two risks are
specific to the self-play recipe. Because terminated games restart from the standard initial position,
a low-temperature, prior-anchored policy could narrow opening diversity over training; persistent root
randomization, as in AlphaZero, is the natural safeguard. Figure 7 quantifies the
narrowing after training—real for every run but far from collapse under any regularizer—though
it measures the policy’s play distribution, not the opening diversity of the games actually
generated. And the
frozen prior is least reliable on exactly the off-distribution states self-play reaches, where forcing
coverage of its support is least justified—the covariate shift reappearing one level up—which
annealing β\beta as the policy drifts would mitigate.

BT4-1024x15x32h-swa-6147500 named in Section 3, a 1515-layer
encoder-only transformer with 10241024-dimensional embeddings, 3232 attention heads, and a

of 15361536. It matches the 191191M-parameter Leela-CF model of Monroe et al. (2026) in

(93.5%93.5\%; Table 6), which is what licenses us to read that work’s rating as this

and destination square representations are multiplied along the embedding axis to form a

The interpretability results we draw on in Section 1 are obtained on a different,
smaller Lc0 transformer of the same square-token lineage—the 768768-dimensional, 2424-head
T82-768x15x24h network (≈109\approx\!109M parameters)
(Sandmann et al., 2025)—not on the checkpoint we fine-tune. It nonetheless shares the
